XTB S.A. Capital Group 2025 Consolidated Annual Report; ESG stakeholder-engagement and double materiality section. Stakeholder framework maps principal stakeholder categories to dialogue methods and engagement objectives: Regulatory environment (KNF, local market supervisors; cyclical reports to KNF, correspondence with KNF, Financial Ombudsman, UOKiK; goal: transparent, responsive regulatory communication and legal/regulatory compliance); Social environment (financial-education audiences, prospective clients, social partners, cultural/sporting-event institutions, universities/schools, XTB Foundation; engagement via product website, investor-relations/ESG site, advertising, social media, educational actions, sponsorship, partnerships, HR fairs; examples: XTB Investing Masterclass conference, XTB IT Academy, webinars/training, Confitura conference, IT Job Fairs, "Szlachetna Paczka" charity action, cooperation with KSW MMA; goal: identify client preferences, tailor XTB offer, strategic partnerships, talent acquisition); Market environment (industry organizations, suppliers, local-market business partners; via trade fairs, direct contact, advertising, meetings/webinars, email; examples: Google Finance Summit (GtFT), Wroclaw letSwift x Toast meetup powered by XTB, JUG meetings Bydgoszcz/Lodz, ngPoznan meetup powered by XTB, Devoxx Poland, CocoaHeads Tricity 2025; goal: durable business relations, knowledge exchange, brand trust); Capital-market representatives (shareholders, individual/institutional investors, Warsaw Stock Exchange, analysts, rating agencies; via current/periodic reporting, e-AGM broadcasts, investor conferences, investor materials, Management Board interviews, IR website, Investor Calendar, cooperation with Association of Individual Investors; goal: align policies with shareholder guidance, adapt reporting, build investor trust, regulatory compliance).

2025 sustainability statement prepared on Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) conducted in 2024 per ESRS standards, revised for currency in 2025 (refs IRO-1/G1, IRO-1/E1, IRO-1). Original 2024 DMA executed in 5 stages; input parameters were identification of key stakeholder groups, processes and value chain. Preparatory stage covered: review of basic company information, analysis of XTB Group business environment, analysis of current sustainability practices, value-chain mapping (upstream/own operations/downstream), identification/description of key stakeholders. Step 2 — cross-sectional stakeholder opinion survey via online questionnaire; respondents: XTB Group employees, XTB S.A. Supervisory Board members, XTB clients, and other stakeholder representatives (suppliers/business partners, local communities/social partners, media representatives, shareholders/investors). Question and participant selection preceded by preparatory workshops on stakeholder and value-chain mapping; two rounds of in-depth interviews conducted — first round with selected online-survey addressees, second round after E/S/G workshops covering key branch and subsidiary representatives. Survey results directly shaped current ESG Strategy, set development directions for environmental, social and governance areas, defined objectives addressing stakeholder needs, and drove decision to intensify XTB Foundation activity, especially in financial education.

Step 3 — preliminary double-materiality analysis: assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities via workshop series evaluating actual/potential impacts on people and environment and Group risks/opportunities on ESG topics per ESRS, based on XTB value-chain elements; 5 E/S/G workshops involved XTB managers, key-area specialists and advisory-firm experts, identifying ESG impacts, risks and opportunities material from enterprise perspective. Step 4 — material-topic selection methodology: impact materiality assessed by probability of occurrence split by time horizon (for potential impacts) and impact severity (scale, scope, character/reversibility of negative effects); financial materiality assessed by probability of risk/opportunity by time horizon and scale of financial consequences upon materialization; materiality thresholds applied.

Most material ESG topics identified by surveyed stakeholders: ENVIRONMENT & CLIMATE — for all stakeholders: responsible e-waste management and minimizing negative climate impact; for employees: same; for suppliers: greenhouse-gas emission reduction and sustainable ICT. SOCIAL — for all: personal-data security/confidentiality, effective employee communication, client service quality and satisfaction; for employees: data security/confidentiality and effective employee communication; for suppliers: effective employee communication. GOVERNANCE — for stakeholders: business ethics, legal/regulatory compliance, anti-corruption practices, countering corruption, bribery and money laundering (materiality emphasized across all stakeholder groups); for clients: fair competition, anti-corruption/bribery/money-laundering countermeasures, business ethics. Stakeholders also flagged Group involvement in education (raising employee environmental awareness and financial-management education for children/youth) and suggested greater Group engagement in charitable/social actions (e.g., tree planting, public-space waste collection).

Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation)_ . W dniu 16 października 2025 r. W oczekiwaniu na zakończenie procesu legislacyjnego, XTB prowadzi prace związane zarówno z opracowaniem niezbędnych dokumentów prawnych, jak i wprowadzaniem technologicznych zmian w aplikacji i platformie XTB, które pozwolą na dodanie kryptoaktywów do oferty. Wprowadzenie opcji do oferty XTB uzależnione jest od akceptacji przez KNF modelu wyceny opcji. Obecnie trwa proces z tym związany, w którym KNF może składać do Spółki dodatkowe pytania do przedstawionych dokumentów. Przedstawiony powyżej plan produktowy odpowiada aktualnemu stanowi wiedzy i zasobów. Realizacja tego planu przez XTB jest uzależniona m.in. od czynników zewnętrznych, które są poza kontrolą Spółki, jak współpraca z zewnętrznymi dostawcami, uzyskanie niezbędnych zgód regulacyjnych czy uchwalenie odpowiednich przepisów prawnych. W związku z tym, plan produktowy może ulec zmianom i modyfikacjom.

XTB S.A. Capital Group Q3 2025 report excerpt (sections 4.5 All-in-One investment app, 4.6 2025 product plan, EU client transaction metrics, Effie Awards 2025). Late October 2025 XTB won gold statuette at prestigious Effie Awards 2025 competition, recognizing marketing effectiveness of advertising campaign run across 2024/2025 turn; campaign drove new-accounts growth dynamics up to ~27%. Top-of-mind brand awareness (first brand respondents recall) rose from 8.4% to 33%; spontaneous brand awareness (recognition without prompts) rose to 41%. Poland is among 55+ global Effie programs; nominated/awarded campaigns enter Effie Index, the global marketing-effectiveness indicator ranking most effective brands, networks and holdings worldwide.

All-in-One investment app strategy: Management ambition for XTB to be associated as leading All-in-One investment app in Europe, offering clients easy, intelligent, efficient ways to trade, invest and save while ensuring instant access to their money. XTB continues transformation from CFD broker into modern FinTech delivering universal investment app; transformation to continue in 2025 and subsequent years.

2025 product plan: Over first nine months of 2025, XTB continued intensive new-client acquisition begun prior year, focused on individuals interested in long-term passive investing and broad financial management, enabled by universal investment app, new products/services, and changes improving comfort of XTB mobile app and platform. Systematic preparation reflected in ongoing development of Product and Technology Division, including development and R&D work tied to responsible deployment of AI-based technologies.

Q1 2025: launch of eWallet service for clients in Poland. Virtual wallet activated by nearly 22k clients (43% in Poland, 57% from abroad). eWallet provides multi-currency card supporting cashless in-store payments, mobile transactions and contactless ATM cash withdrawals worldwide; supports accounts in 25 currencies including EUR, USD, GBP, PLN, HUF, RON, CZK, CHF, JPY, CAD, BRL, INR, LKR, plus fast free inter-account transfers. Instant access to funds; card issued under Mastercard license by DiPocket UAB, an Electronic Money Institution registered by Bank of Lithuania. eWallet currently available to clients from Poland, Czechia, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Germany, France, Spain and Italy.

Late March 2025: announced product changes for long-term saving/retirement categories. In Poland, pending orders added within IKE (Individual Retirement Account) responding to XTB client demand. UK clients given ability to transfer existing ISA (Individual Savings Account) to XTB — whole account or partial assets.

Q2 2025: launch of PEA accounts (Plan d'Epargne en Actions) for clients in France. PEA holders may invest in equities and ETP funds with favorable tax treatment such as capital-gains income tax exemption if investments held in account at least 5 years. Maximum PEA contribution limit EUR 150k per client.

Q3 2025: XTB introduced long-awaited IKZE account (Individual Retirement Security Account) for Polish clients. IKZE available to any individual (non-shareable account), including sole proprietors, who is 16+ and has Polish tax residence. IKZE gains exempt from 19% capital-gains tax; accumulated capital is inheritable. Account subject to annual contribution limit deductible from income in tax return. Withdrawals permitted after age 65 and meeting condition of contributions across at least 5 calendar years — then taxed at flat-rate income tax of 10%. Without meeting these conditions, funds may be refunded from IKZE but with tax per the tax scale applicable in the given year.

XTB continues universal investment-app strategy targeting every investor seeking to manage funds effectively, short- and long-term; plans portfolio expansion with further products. In first three quarters of 2025 the team focused on preparing to introduce cryptocurrencies and options.

Cryptocurrency introduction strictly tied to and contingent on completion in Poland of legislative process enacting law aligning Polish regulations with MiCA Regulation (Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation). On 16 October 2025 the Senate reviewed the draft bill, submitted amendments, and referred it to the Public Finance Committee, which on 6 November 2025 adopted some amendments and returned the bill to the Sejm. Pending legislative completion, XTB conducts work on required legal documents and technological changes to XTB app and platform enabling addition of crypto-assets to offering.

Options introduction contingent on KNF (Polish FSA) acceptance of option-pricing model; related process ongoing, with KNF able to submit additional questions on submitted documents.

Stated product plan reflects current state of knowledge and resources; execution depends on external factors beyond Company control (cooperation with external providers, obtaining necessary regulatory approvals, enactment of relevant legal provisions) and may be subject to changes and modifications.

Undiscounted projected collection schedule from receivables packages totals 26,152.0M PLN at 31.12.2025 vs 23,147.2M PLN at 31.12.2024; near-term tranches: up to 12 months 3,602.6M PLN (2024: 3,304.7M), 1-2 years 3,341.0M PLN (3,091.8M), 2-3 years 2,904.1M PLN (2,656.7M), 3-4 years 2,484.1M PLN (2,219.3M), 4-5 years 2,110.6M PLN (1,922.6M), declining stepwise to 506.9M PLN (432.9M) for 14-15 years, with above-15-years tranche 1,177.5M PLN (1,091.8M). Schedule shifts across comparative periods due to acquisition of new receivables portfolios, realization of cash inflows from held portfolios, and revision of projected future cash inflows.

Net carrying value of investment in receivables packages rose to 11,632.7M PLN at 31.12.2025 (unsecured 10,804.2M + secured 828.5M) from opening 10,500.3M PLN at 01.01.2025 (unsecured 9,674.6M + secured 825.7M). 2025 movements: portfolio purchases +2,222.9M PLN (unsecured 2,057.2M, secured 165.7M); disposal from sale of subsidiary (2.4M PLN); collections from debtors and portfolio sales (3,919.7M PLN) (unsecured 3,562.8M, secured 357.0M); increase in liabilities to debtors for overpayments +5.9M PLN; loyalty program valuation +1.8M PLN; collection revenue from purchased portfolios +2,898.2M PLN (unsecured 2,698.5M, secured 199.7M); value of repossessed properties (1.8M PLN); FX translation differences on receivables (72.4M PLN) (unsecured (68.6M), secured (3.8M)). 2024 comparative: opening 8,673.8M PLN (01.01.2024), purchases 2,827.9M PLN, collections (3,536.3M PLN), overpayment liabilities +4.3M PLN, loyalty program (1.4M PLN), payments from original creditor (1.9M PLN), collection revenue 2,637.6M PLN, repossessed properties (3.6M PLN), FX (100.0M PLN), closing 10,500.3M PLN. Purchase-price entry includes acquisition-cost adjustment for discount on defective cases. Receivables value adjusted for loyalty program valuation and change in overpayment liabilities, recognized under Other income/costs from purchased portfolios. End of August 2024 KRUK Group completed the "Marzenia do spełnienia" loyalty program, reversing the points provision of 8,952k PLN (9.0M PLN). FX differences relate to non-PLN portfolios, mainly EUR/PLN fluctuations.

Primary activity of Parent and most subsidiaries is investment in acquired receivables portfolios; per IAS 7.15 treated as core operating activity, acquisition expenditures presented as Change in investment in receivables packages within operating cash flow. Group occasionally disposes of individual cases from portfolios to boost core operating revenue. In current period KRUK Group sold receivables portfolios in Czech and Slovak markets as part of scaling back activity on those markets; per IAS 7.14 sale proceeds presented within operating activities as Change in investment in receivables packages. 2025 expenditure on portfolio purchases 2,222.9M PLN (2024: 2,827.9M PLN); collections from debtors 3,919.7M PLN (2024: 3,536.3M PLN).

Cumulative expected credit losses on purchased receivables portfolios increased to 4,645.3M PLN at 31.12.2025 from opening 3,924.8M PLN (vs 2024: closing 3,924.8M from opening 3,189.3M). 2025 movements: update of inflow forecast +496.9M PLN (unsecured 514.0M, secured (17.1M); 2024: +390.1M, unsecured 397.5M, secured (7.4M)); deviations from actual payments and reductions from earlier realization on secured cases +223.6M PLN (unsecured 149.0M, secured 74.6M; 2024: +345.5M, unsecured 296.3M, secured 49.2M). ECL changes reflected in portfolio carrying value.

Granted loans totaled 612.3M PLN at 31.12.2025 vs 502.9M PLN at 31.12.2024, comprising loans measured at amortized cost 610.0M PLN (2024: 499.6M PLN) and loans measured at fair value 2.3M PLN (2024: 3.3M PLN).

output: Dom Development S.A. and its Capital Group 2025 Management Report, Consolidated Sustainability Reporting Section 3, Climate Risk Analysis. Transition (technological, market, legal) and physical climate risks for residential development operations are mapped to potential financial impacts and mitigation measures. Technological-change risks: digitalization exposures (cybersecurity, business-continuity assurance, unauthorized data access); misalignment of IT systems with business and regulatory needs; requirement to incorporate renewable (OZE) heat-supply sources into investments; substitution of materials, equipment and fleet with lower-emission options; mandated low-emission materials and zero-emission building construction; engagement in innovations such as long-term renewable Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs); potential shortening of asset life cycles causing earlier impairment, withdrawal or write-off of high-emission machinery, equipment and fleet; and rising costs from potential full fleet electrification. Market and legal risks: dynamics and quality of legal change; dependence of debt financing on ESG/CO2 regulation; dependence of company financial standing on overall sector condition; market shifts from increased supply; loss of financial liquidity; too-slow or failed compliance with expectations; rising costs of raw materials, materials and services; rising electrical and thermal energy prices driven by Poland's high-emission energy mix; difficulty attracting and retaining clients, employees, business partners and investors as environmental issues gain importance and activities are deemed climate-harmful. Identified revenue risks include lost revenue from failing client requirements, changing client requirements versus current product portfolio, and construction work interruptions; increased costs from energy and raw-material price volatility and spending on new climate-friendly business processes; offset by revenue-increase opportunities via access to new market segments and easier attraction/retention of skilled workers. Mitigants: assessing profitability of development projects using low-emission materials and technologies; building capability through training in low-emission design and new-technology use; price sensitivity assessments and contingency plans for central procurement; developing capacity to meet client preferences and improving value-chain collaboration; product, material and technology portfolio diversification, broader low-emission material sourcing, supplier cooperation and circular-economy options; review of insurance arrangements and monitoring of the insurance market; assessment of physical climate-risk exposure for assets and projects near waterways and coasts; increasing facility resilience to extreme weather through improved protections and adaptive solutions; consideration of development-project siting; conducting client-preference research and analysis (NPS); and signing long-term contracts with multiple external suppliers. Physical risks: Group companies manage physical risks for development projects using climate-change scenarios for Poland in the 21st century prepared by IOS-PIB under the Klimada 2.0 project, RCP 8.5 scenario (assuming continuation of current GHG-emission growth) compared with the 2011-2020 decade, and Municipal Adaptation Plans (klimada2.ios.gov.pl/klimat-scenariusze; access date 01.02.2024). Acute risk from extreme weather - increased rainfall and torrential rain (annual rainfall sum, number of days per year with precipitation >20mm): hazards include greater probability of local flooding from irregular rainfall and probability of flash floods in cities; potential financial effects include impairment and early asset withdrawal due to property damage, reduced insurance availability for high-risk-location assets, higher insurance premiums from greater adaptation spending and stricter policy terms, and reduced revenue from production declines or supply-chain interruptions. Mitigation: investment in blue infrastructure and nature-based solutions; implementation of best practices and water-management instruments; development of weather-resilient construction technology; increasing micro-retention (building small ponds and reservoirs); preventive and awareness actions on correct workplace behavior; and appropriate material storage. Acute risk from heat waves (number of hot and sweltering days): hazards include increased frequency of combined-sewer storm overflows and increased volume of wastewater discharged to receivers; effects include higher stormwater/combined-sewage pumping costs, need for new water-and-sewage infrastructure and stormwater-management investment solutions, contaminated surface runoff, infrastructure damage (e.g., flooding of transformer stations), rising groundwater levels, sewer-network inadequacy, and impacts on building waterproofing and dampness. Further heat-related effects: reduced revenue and higher costs from negative impacts on employees (health, safety, absenteeism); higher property taxes (cleanup and mitigation costs); and higher margins from increased risk. Additional physical-risk consequences identified: possible interruption of electricity supply in summer and winter periods; water-access limitations causing changes in material/service availability and prices; need to modify work schedules due to intensified weather phenomena; possible reduced profitability of investments located in elevated-environmental-risk areas; possible impairment of land-bank assets; constraints on location availability for development projects; and potential limitations on building-material availability.

The Ordinary General Meeting also sets the dividend record date and dividend payment date; record date may be the date of the profit-distribution resolution or within the following three months. Amount distributable to shareholders may not exceed profit for the last financial year, increased by undistributed profits from prior years and amounts transferred from supplementary and reserve capitals created from profit that may be allocated to dividends; this amount must be reduced by uncovered losses, treasury shares, and amounts that under the Commercial Companies Code or the Articles of Association must be allocated from the last financial year's profit to supplementary or reserve capital. The Management Board may pay shareholders an advance toward the anticipated year-end dividend if the Company holds sufficient funds; advance payment requires Supervisory Board consent and is permitted only if the approved financial statements for the prior financial year show a profit. The advance may not exceed half of profit earned since the end of the prior financial year as shown in audited financial statements, increased by reserve capitals created from profit available to the Management Board for advance payments and reduced by uncovered losses and treasury shares. Dividend rights accrue to persons holding dematerialized bearer Shares recorded in their accounts on the dividend record date and to parties entitled from dematerialized Shares recorded in an omnibus account. A shareholder's claim against the Company for dividend payment may be enforced within 10 years from the date of the Ordinary General Meeting resolution.

Pre-emptive rights: the Management Board presents the General Meeting a written opinion justifying disapplication of pre-emptive rights and the proposed issue price of new shares or method of determining it. A resolution disapplying shareholders' pre-emptive rights requires a majority of at least four-fifths of votes. These requirements do not apply where: the capital-increase resolution provides that new shares are to be subscribed in full by a financial institution (underwriter/subemitent) obligated to subsequently offer them to shareholders to enable exercise of pre-emptive rights on terms set in the resolution; or the resolution provides that new shares are to be subscribed by an underwriter where shareholders entitled to pre-emptive rights do not subscribe for part or all of the shares offered to them.

Right to share in assets on liquidation: on Company liquidation, assets remaining after satisfaction or securing of creditors are divided among shareholders in proportion to contributions made by each to the share capital.

Right to participate in the General Meeting and voting rights: shareholders exercise voting rights at General Meetings, which under the Commercial Companies Code may be ordinary or extraordinary. Each Share carries one vote at the General Meeting. A shareholder may participate and vote in person or by proxy; a shareholder intending to act through a proxy must grant the proxy authority in writing or electronic form, and the Company takes steps to identify the shareholder and proxy to verify the validity of electronic proxies (detailed verification procedures are set out in the General Meeting convening notice). Per the Articles, participation via electronic means of communication is permitted where the convening notice states such possibility, in which case the Company must enable electronic participation; detailed rules are set by the Management Board consistent with the General Meeting Regulations and published on the Company website with the convening notice. A shareholder holding shares recorded in more than one securities account may appoint separate proxies for each account. Where the proxy is a Management Board member, Supervisory Board member, liquidator, Company employee, or a member of governing bodies or employee of a subsidiary company or cooperative, the proxy may authorize representation at only one General Meeting.

The list of persons entitled to participate in the General Meeting is determined from a register prepared by the securities depository operator under the Act on Trading in Financial Instruments and from the state disclosed in the Company's share register on the participation record date. The list is displayed at the Company's registered office for three days preceding the General Meeting; a shareholder may request the list be sent free of charge by email to a provided address. For shares recorded in an omnibus account, entitlement is confirmed by a certificate issued by the account holder; where the omnibus account is operated by KDPW (or a KDPW-engaged entity for depository duties), information on the account holder must be provided to KDPW by the omnibus-account operator before the first such issuance. The omnibus-account holder prepares the list of persons authorized to participate; if not a KDPW participant (or KDPW-engaged bank), the list is delivered via a KDPW participant or KDPW-engaged bank. A shareholder may transfer Shares in the period between the participation record date and the close of the General Meeting.

KRUK Group H1 2025 condensed interim consolidated financial statements (półroczny). Net finance costs reached PLN 218.7M in H1 2025, up PLN 34.0M versus H1 2024, driven by higher debt (debt balance rose PLN 1,016.9M). Expenditure on new debt portfolio acquisitions totaled PLN 805.5M in H1 2025, down 10% from PLN 899.7M in the prior-year period. Collections from acquired portfolios reached PLN 1,910.3M in H1 2025, up 10% year-over-year; over half of payments came from foreign markets. The PLN 172.8M increase in collections versus H1 2024 was driven mainly by PLN 72.2M higher payments on the Italian market (+19% y/y) and PLN 42.5M higher on the Polish market (+6% y/y). Russian aggression on Ukraine: the situation in Ukraine does not affect positions presented in the financial statements as at the balance sheet date, nor recognition or measurement of items after the balance sheet date.

Note 15 – issuance, redemption and repayment of non-equity and equity securities: During 1 January–30 June 2025 the Group redeemed bonds per issue terms: series AL2 on 2 February 2025, nominal PLN 52.5M (second redemption installment); series AE4 on 27 March 2025, nominal PLN 115.0M; series AH1 on 28 June 2025, nominal PLN 50.0M. New bond issues in the same period: AP3 unsecured bonds on 5 February 2025, nominal PLN 100.0M, floating rate WIBOR3M plus 2.80 p.p. margin, maturity 5 February 2031; AL5 unsecured bonds on 2 June 2025, nominal PLN 400.0M, floating rate WIBOR3M plus 3.00 p.p. margin, maturity 2 June 2032. On 12 June 2025 the Management Board of KRUK S.A. adopted a resolution establishing the XII Bond Issue Program with total nominal value not exceeding PLN 900.0M, under which the Parent may issue public bonds. After the reporting period, under the XI Bond Issue Program, AP4 unsecured bonds were issued on 7 July 2025, nominal PLN 100.0M, floating rate WIBOR3M plus 2.70 p.p. margin, maturity 7 July 2031.

Note 16 – dividend paid (or declared): On 23 June 2025 the Ordinary General Meeting of KRUK S.A., per the Management Board's recommendation, resolved to pay a dividend to Parent shareholders of PLN 18.00 per share. The dividend payout of PLN 349,252,434.00 will be made from the Parent's 2024 net profit. The record date for shareholders entitled to dividend for the financial year ended 31 December 2024 was set at 10 July 2025. The dividend covered 19,402,913 KRUK S.A. shares. Dividend payment date set at 25 September 2025. The Group's 2024 profit will be distributed under KRUK S.A.'s Dividend Policy adopted by the Parent's Management Board on 2 December 2021. On 16 January 2025 the Parent's Management Board adopted a resolution accepting KRUK S.A.'s Dividend Policy for financial years from the year beginning 1 January 2025 through the year ending 31 December 2029. Per the adopted Policy, KRUK S.A.'s objective is sustained development and growth of Group value yielding profit growth and dividend payments, while maintaining adequate financial liquidity and respecting ESG sustainability principles. The Management Board assumes it will submit to the Ordinary General Meeting a dividend recommendation of at least 30% of the consolidated net profit of the KRUK Group earned in the prior financial year attributable to Parent shareholders, provided that debt including the recommended dividend does not exceed 3.0 net debt/cash EBITDA. The Dividend Policy is available on the Issuer's website at https://pl.KRUK.eu/relacje inwestorskie/polityka dywidendowa.

Note 17 addresses changes in contingent liabilities or contingent assets since the end of the last financial year (heading only).

# **3 SKONSOLIDOWANA SPRAWOZDAWCZOŚĆ ZRÓWNOWAŻONEGO ROZWOJU**
## **E4-1 PLAN TRANSFORMACJI W ZAKRESIE RÓŻNORODNOŚCI BIOLOGICZNEJ I EKOSYSTEMÓW ORAZ UWZGLĘDNIENIE RÓŻNORODNOŚCI BIOLOGICZNEJ EKOSYSTEMÓW W STRATEGII I MODELU BIZNESOWYM**
Grupa Dom Development nie posiada planu transformacji w zakresie różnorodności biologicznej i ekosystemów. Grupa opracuje plan transformacji nie wcześniej niż w 2030 r. Grupa nie przeprowadziła analizy odporności strategii biznesowej i modelu biznesowego w odniesieniu do różnorodności biologicznej i ekosystemów.  
Grupa prowadzi działalność i realizuje swoje inwestycje wyłącznie na terenie Polski, co sprawia, że podejście do kwestii różnorodności biologicznej jest stabilne w wymiarze prawnym. Jeden z filarów modelu biznesowego opiera się na rozwoju z uwzględnieniem zrównoważonego rozwoju, co przekłada się na działania zgodne z przepisami w zakresie ochrony przyrody.

# **3 SKONSOLIDOWANA SPRAWOZDAWCZOŚĆ ZRÓWNOWAŻONEGO ROZWOJU**
## **E4- 2 POLITYKI ZWIĄZANE Z RÓŻNORODNOŚCIĄ BIOLOGICZNĄ I EKOSYSTEMAMI**
Grupa nie posiada odrębnej polityki adresującej zagadnienie różnorodności biologicznej  
i ekosystemów. Opracowanie odrębnej polityki zaplanowano nie wcześniej niż na rok 2030.

# **3 SKONSOLIDOWANA SPRAWOZDAWCZOŚĆ ZRÓWNOWAŻONEGO ROZWOJU**
## **E4-3 DZIAŁANIA I ZASOBY ZWIĄZANE Z RÓŻNORODNOŚCIĄ BIOLOGICZNĄ I EKOSYSTEMAMI**
Grupa w swoich działaniach stosuje sekwencyjny model stosowany, oznaczający hierarchię łagodzenia wpływu na środowisko i zmniejszenia szkód dla różnorodności biologicznej. Model ten wskazuje kolejno: zapobieganie skutkom (unikanie), ograniczanie nieuniknionych szkód (minimalizacja), naprawianie szkód na miejscu (przywracanie), a tylko w ostateczności wymagane prawnie kompensowanie strat (kompensacja).  
Będąc świadomym wpływu działalności deweloperskiej na środowisko naturalne, spółki z Grupy promują i włączają się w działania mające na celu rewitalizację obszarów, które były wcześniej wykorzystywane do innych celów (m.in. przemysłowych). Tego rodzaju tereny często są zlokalizowane w pobliżu infrastruktury komunikacyjnej i usługowej, wobec czego ich rewitalizacja, m.in. poprzez wprowadzenie funkcji mieszkaniowej, wpływa także na ograniczenie szkodliwego zjawiska tzw. rozlewania się miast. W Strategii DOM 2030 Grupa zadeklarowała realizację projektów rewitalizacyjnych, w ramach, których odzyskiwane będą „zapomniane” i niedostępne dla mieszkańców obszary miast. Przykładem takiego projektu, realizowanym od 2024 r., jest inwestycja zlokalizowana przy ul. Rydlówka 5 na krakowskim Podgórzu.  
Grupa zrealizowała ponad 1100 mieszkań na terenach zdegradowanych, które zostały przywrócone miastom i ich mieszkańcom.  
Spółki z Grupy nie uwzględniły wiedzy społeczności lokalnych, a także nie dokonały analizy skutków finansowych działań wyrównujących.  
Do działań opartych na zasobach przyrody, które spółki z Grupy realizują w inwestycjach, na podstawie wewnętrznego standardu, tj. Zielonej Karty Inwestycji, należą m.in.: zielone dachy, ogrody deszczowe, redukcja efektu miejskiej wyspy ciepła. Działania podejmowane przez spółki z Grupy nie są częścią szerszego planu działań zbiorowych ani planów współpracy regionalnej.  
Zgodnie z celem wyznaczonym w Strategii ESG DOM 2030 Grupa Dom Development, w 2024 r. oficjalnie rozpoczęła realizację programu „Miejska Zieleń”. Działania podejmowane w ramach realizacji tego celu są systematyczną, coroczną praktyką realizowaną przez spółki na każdym z rynków Grupy. Jego celem jest zagospodarowanie co najmniej jednego ogólnodostępnego terenu w aglomeracjach, w których działają spółki z Grupy. W 2025 roku Grupa Dom Development przeznaczyła  
Zdegradowane tereny poprzemysłowe zostały zamienione w nowe przestrzenie również na Osiedlu Urbino, Osiedlu Bokserska i Apartamentach Literacka w Warszawie oraz w Gdańsku na ul. Kartuskiej i na Dolnym Mieście przy ul. Jaskółczej, Jałmużniczej oraz Kurzej. Łącznie, w 2025 roku  
na ogólnodostępne zielone tereny blisko 8 mln zł[18] (vs. 6 mln zł w 2024 roku), co przełożyło się na ponad 1,5 ha nowych terenów zieleni w czterech aglomeracjach Polski. Dzięki inicjatywie:  
- na warszawskim Chrzanowie powstał park, w sąsiedztwie Dzielnicy Mieszkaniowej Metro Zachód,  
- uporządkowany został teren przy Górce Tarnogajskiej oraz nasadzenia przy ul. Zielnej we Wrocławiu,  
- przy ul. Malborskiej w Krakowie powstał park kieszonkowy,  
- w Gdańsku zrealizowano park kieszonkowy przy ul. Lema, skwer przy skrzyżowaniu ulic Piekarniczej i Lema oraz nowe nabrzeże Motławy na Dolnym Mieście.  
W uzasadnionych przypadkach[19] spółki z Grupy są zobligowane do przeprowadzania remediacji, której sposób określony jest w decyzjach administracyjnych wydawanych przez regionalne  
organy ochrony środowiska. Każdorazowo usunięty zanieczyszczony grunt przekazywany jest do dalszego zagospodarowania uprawnionym podmiotom poza terenem jego wytworzenia, w jego miejsce zostaje nawieziony czysty grunt.  
Spółki z Grupy, zgodnie z decyzjami administracyjnymi, dokonują nasadzeń kompensacyjnych. Działania te realizowane są punktowo w ramach inwestycji, a nie jako formalne offsety.

output: Grupa Dom Development consolidated sustainability report (ESRS E4 biodiversity and ecosystems disclosures). E4-1 transition plan: Group has no biodiversity/ecosystems transition plan and will develop one no earlier than 2030; no resilience analysis of business strategy/model versus biodiversity and ecosystems was performed. Operations and investments confined exclusively to Poland, rendering the legal approach to biodiversity stable; one business-model pillar rests on sustainable-development-oriented growth aligned with nature-protection regulations. E4-2 policies: Group has no separate biodiversity/ecosystems policy; development of a dedicated policy planned no earlier than 2030. E4-3 actions and resources: Group applies the sequential mitigation hierarchy—prevention (avoidance), limiting unavoidable harm (minimization), on-site restoration, and only as a last resort legally required compensation (offsetting). Group companies promote and engage in revitalization of formerly used (e.g. industrial) areas, typically located near transport and service infrastructure; such revitalization, including introduction of residential function, curbs urban sprawl. Under Strategy DOM 2030 the Group committed to revitalization projects recovering "forgotten" and inaccessible urban areas; example project ongoing since 2024 located at ul. Rydlówka 5 in Kraków's Podgórze district. Group delivered over 1,100 apartments on degraded land returned to cities and residents. Group companies did not incorporate local-community knowledge and did not analyze financial effects of remediation/compensation actions. Nature-based actions implemented per internal standard (Green Investment Card / Zielona Karta Inwestycji) include green roofs, rain gardens, and urban heat-island reduction; these actions are not part of any broader collective action plan or regional cooperation plans. Per ESG Strategy DOM 2030 target, the Group officially launched the "Miejska Zieleń" (Urban Greenery) program in 2024 as a systematic annual practice across all Group markets, aiming to develop at least one publicly accessible area in each agglomeration where Group companies operate. Degraded post-industrial sites also transformed into new spaces at Osiedle Urbino, Osiedle Bokserska, and Apartamenty Literacka in Warsaw, and in Gdańsk on ul. Kartuska and in the Dolne Miasto (Lower Town) area on ul. Jaskółcza, Jałmużnicza, and Kurza. In 2025 the Group allocated nearly PLN 8 million to publicly accessible green areas (versus PLN 6 million in 2024), translating into over 1.5 ha of new green areas across four Polish agglomerations. Through this initiative: a park was created in Warsaw's Chrzanów neighborhood adjacent to the Metro Zachód residential district; the area near Górka Tarnogajska was tidied and plantings made on ul. Zielna in Wrocław; a pocket park was created on ul. Malborska in Kraków; and in Gdańsk a pocket park on ul. Lema, a square at the Piekarnicza/Lema intersection, and a new Motława waterfront in the Lower Town were delivered. In justified cases Group companies are obliged to conduct remediation in the manner defined by administrative decisions issued by regional environmental-protection authorities; removed contaminated soil is transferred for further management to authorized entities off-site and replaced with clean soil. Per administrative decisions, Group companies perform compensatory plantings, implemented on a point basis within investments rather than as formal offsets. In 2025, in assessing the Group's environmental impact, an inventory was conducted of investments located in flood-prone areas of low flood risk (i.e. in the event of total destruction of flood embankments); in 2025, 25% of investments were located in floodplain areas, with identification of adaptive measures for such projects deferred to the following year. E4-4 targets: Group has not set measurable, outcome-oriented biodiversity and ecosystems targets, as current targets, actions, and plans are covered by the ESG Strategy DOM 2030; additional ambitions concern the "Miejska Zieleń" program and revitalization (detailed in E4-3). Group will set such targets no earlier than 2030. Targets relating to delivery of publicly accessible green areas and investments on degraded land were not based on global biodiversity frameworks, did not apply ecological thresholds, and assigned no impact attribution in their determination.

output: XTB S.A. Capital Group 2025 Consolidated Annual Report excerpt detailing risk-factor catalogue, mitigation, and internal capital adequacy framework. Risk VI Business Risk: failure to achieve required economic targets due to competitive losses; sub-risks include adverse competitive conditions (higher operating costs/lower revenue from client attrition), client outflow to competitors amid low market volatility, low inflation, and insufficiently responsive costly marketing campaigns, plus adverse economic-social shifts reducing revenue via lower net client deposits, reduced client risk appetite, and migration of investments to low-risk bonds/bank deposits. Mitigation: continuous competitive-environment monitoring, competitiveness risk management, cost-control/controlling actions, ongoing trading-result monitoring, and ESG Strategy. Risk VII Environmental and Climate Risk: losses tied to climate change, energy access, extreme weather, and ESG compliance. Physical/climate business-continuity risk: severe weather (floods, hurricanes) at Group branch locations threatening employee safety and local office equipment, causing temporary localized client-service disruptions and cost increases, without affecting core trading-platform stability (housed in secure zones); mitigated via geographic office diversification, critical IT infrastructure in low-risk locations, immediate remote-work readiness, physical equipment safeguards, and BCP/DR plans and drills. Energy availability/cost risk (outages, price spikes affecting office/IT upkeep): higher operating costs, supply-interruption risk to service availability, possible indirect client service disruptions; mitigated via power-continuity contracts/procedures (UPS/aggregation at critical sites), server energy-efficiency optimization, renewable (OZE) energy where feasible, and supply cost/risk monitoring. ESG regulatory non-alignment risk (EU/local rules: CSRD Directive, EU Taxonomy, non-financial reporting): exposure to administrative penalties, regulator sanctions, higher legal/ESG-data-audit costs, and credibility loss among institutional investors increasingly conditioning capital decisions on sustainability metrics; mitigated via adoption and execution of the ESG Strategy 2024-2027 (setting concrete corporate-governance and environmental targets), legal-environment monitoring, external sustainability-reporting experts, internal control and Compliance, and full carbon-footprint calculation enabling precise emissions reporting/management. Market/social negative-perception risk (inaction on climate, social-irresponsibility or greenwashing perception): potential investor (shareholder) outflow, financing difficulties, and client loss—especially younger-generation clients for whom environmental criteria drive provider selection; mitigated via publication of Sustainability Statement and climate policy, OZE energy purchase (confirmed by Guarantees of Origin for the Warsaw headquarters), promotion of rational resource use, document digitization, and responsible e-waste management. Risk-classification methodology: factors assigned to risk categories by characteristics, then assessed for materiality into three classes—permanently material, material, and immaterial. Permanently material risks: currency risk, commodity-price risk, and instrument-price risk (classified as market risk); technological and technical risk and legal risk (operational risk); and counterparty risk (credit risk). Management deems these to continuously and materially affect results given business specifics, complexity, resources, and operations. Other risks assessed for materialization impact on incurring material loss or serious operational disruption; deemed material if one materiality criterion met: materialization of a material loss already occurring in XTB activity; stress-test results indicating high loss levels under a risk-realization scenario; recognition as material by the Risk Committee (composed of XTB Supervisory Board members); or designation as critical by business units in the risk self-assessment process. Internal Capital and Liquid-Assets Adequacy Assessment: the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) is a risk-management mechanism—a risk-based process covering all risk types the Company poses to others and is exposed to, assessing both actual and potential risks, incorporating internal factors and regulatory, economic, and business-environment factors. Its output sets the capital level needed to safeguard the Company by covering all material risks. First ICAAP stage: risk identification via comprehensive review of internal/external threats tied to operations, services, processes, and the legal, macroeconomic, and competitive environment given available resources, assessed for probability and potential materialization losses. The XTB risk-management system identifies risks whose materialization could cause financial losses or threaten Company stability, covering internal factors (activity characteristics, services, products, resources) and external factors (macroeconomic situation, competitive environment).

Creotech Instruments S.A. interim report for the 9-month period ended 30 September 2025 (all amounts in thousands PLN unless stated). IFRS standards adoption: amendments effective from 1 January 2024 and EU-approved comprise IFRS 16 Leases (lease liabilities in sale-and-leaseback, published 21 November 2023); IAS 1 Presentation of Financial Statements (classification of liabilities as current/non-current, published 20 December 2023); IAS 7 Statement of Cash Flows and IFRS 7 Financial Instruments disclosures (supplier finance arrangements); Annual Improvements to IFRS Volume 11 (amendments to IFRS 1, IFRS 7, IFRS 9, IFRS 10, IAS 7); and IFRS 9/IFRS 7 amendments on nature-dependent electricity contracts. Published but not yet EU-endorsed: IFRS 9/IFRS 7 classification and measurement amendments (effective annual periods from 1 January 2026); IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements (from 1 January 2027); IFRS 19 Subsidiaries without Public Accountability: Disclosures (from 1 January 2027); IAS 21 amendments on lack of exchangeability (from 1 January 2025). These changes have no material impact on the Company's interim condensed financial statements.

Accounting policy changes vs 31 December 2024: Property, plant and equipment - minimum economic useful life for other fixed assets raised from 1 year to 13 months. PP&E useful-life ranges: Buildings and structures 7-67 years; Technical equipment and machinery 3-10 years; Means of transport 5-15 years; Other fixed assets 13 months-10 years. Inventories - measurement of inventory issues changed to FIFO or specific identification method (issue valued at actual price of each consumed asset where project/contractual requirements apply); cost of non-interchangeable items and goods/services produced for specific projects determined by specific identification of individual purchase prices/production costs. Policy changes have no material impact on current or prior financial statements.

Financial and operating results: Revenue for 9 months ended 30 September 2025 reached PLN 95.1M, up PLN 72.1M year-over-year, driven by progress on the "Mikroglob" project. Total operating costs rose PLN 59.7M to PLN 99.8M; largest drivers were external services (+PLN 43.9M, mainly subcontractor costs on "Mikroglob") and salaries/social security (+PLN 9.8M, reflecting increased scale of operations).

Material P&L items (01.01-30.09.2025 vs 01.01-30.09.2024, thousands PLN): Revenue from product sales 84,608 vs 15,497; Grant/subsidy income 10,462 vs 7,464; Materials and energy consumption 6,742 vs 6,182; External services 50,397 vs 6,515; Salaries, social security and other benefits 31,400 vs 21,562; Depreciation/amortization 10,596 vs 5,976; Net loss from continuing operations -3,043 vs -14,549 (loss narrowed by PLN 11,506k).

Balance sheet: Total assets at 30 September 2025 were PLN 317.0M, up PLN 154.6M vs 31 December 2024. Non-current assets PLN 120.2M, up PLN 12.7M, mainly from a PLN 6.5M increase in intangible assets (capitalized development expenditure). Current assets up PLN 141.9M, driven by a PLN 47.5M rise in contract assets and a PLN 75.7M increase in cash from the series K share issue proceeds and advances received on the "Camila" and "Mikroglob" projects. Equity at 30 September 2025 was PLN 140.7M, up PLN 69.8M from end-2024 due to series K issue proceeds. Trade and other payables rose PLN 71.9M versus end-2024, linked to commencement of key procurement and advances for the "Mikroglob" and "Camila" projects.

Changes in business/economic conditions affecting fair value of financial assets and liabilities: none occurred during the period ended 30 September 2025.

Dom Development S.A. Capital Group corporate report excerpt covering construction pipeline, land bank, and Management Board changes (data as at 31.12.2025 vs 31.12.2024). Na dzień 30 czerwca 2025 roku bank ziemi Grupy – obejmujący zarówno tereny w trakcie przygotowań inwestycyjnych, jak i działki już zabezpieczone – liczył niespełna 19 tys. lokali na czterech głównych rynkach działalności: w Warszawie, Trójmieście, Wrocławiu i Krakowie. Zarząd Spółki ocenia ten

Dzięki posiadanym zasobom gruntów Grupa może w sposób płynny i elastyczny uzupełniać swoją ofertę, odpowiadając na bieżące potrzeby rynkowe oraz utrzymując wiodącą pozycję na krajowym rynku deweloperskim. Zarząd Spółki przywiązuje dużą wagę do stałego zabezpieczania portfela gruntów na wszystkich rynkach, na których prowadzona jest działalność Grupy. Grupa Kapitałowa Dom Development S.A. H1 2025 operational review covering land acquisition, awards, and sustainability risks. Land bank: systematic, predictable acquisition of attractive development land at competitive purchase prices to sustain satisfactory sales margins remains a key success factor and competitive advantage amid limited supply of land with regulated legal/planning status in attractive urban locations. As at 30 June 2025 the Group's land bank (sites in investment preparation plus already secured plots) totaled just under 19,000 units across four core markets: Warsaw, Tri-City, Wrocław and Kraków. Management deems this level appropriate given lengthy administrative procedures, regulatory volatility affecting investment preparation, and housing-finance market conditions. Land reserves enable flexible offer replenishment and maintenance of leading position in the national developer market; acquisition effectiveness rests on long-standing acquisition team experience and a strong liquidity position permitting rapid execution of even large land transactions.

Awards (H1 2025): In the 26th edition of "Puls Biznesu" Giełdowa Spółka Roku 2024 (Listed Company of the Year) ranking, Dom Development placed 3rd in the Management Board Competencies category, reflecting high ratings from analysts, institutional investors, brokers and fund managers. In the "Gwiazdy Rankingu Buildera" listing, based on 2019–2023 financial data, the Group was awarded in four categories: Largest revenues, Largest profit, Consistently at the top, and Largest revenues in the Mazovian voivodeship. In the "Wizjery" competition (Morizon-Gratka Group), the company received a special award for "Outstanding partnership and strategic impact on real-estate market development" and a distinction for "Lifetime achievement in the real-estate market for a developer"; Tri-City Group company Euro Styl won the "Best investment visualization" category. In the RynekPierwotny.pl Ranking Inwestycji 2024, four Group projects ranked among the most popular investments in their agglomerations: Mokotów Sportowy (Warsaw), Braniborska 80 (Wrocław), Apartamenty Park Matecznego (Kraków), and DOKI Living (Gdańsk). In "Builder" monthly's TopBuilder 2025 competition, Stage I of Warsaw's Apartamenty Literacka, delivered by Dom Construction, was honored. Under the ESG DOM 2030 Strategy, the "Odpowiedzialny biznes w Polsce 2024. Dobre praktyki" report (Forum Odpowiedzialnego Biznesu) featured three 2024 Dom Development initiatives: the "Bez barier" apartment finishing service for persons with limited mobility, the "Miejska Zieleń" planting/site revitalization program, and the Wrocław "Dobra Przestrzeń" student architectural competition. The Group was also nominated in the CSR Poland Awards, Community Engagement category, for a housing project for Ukrainian internally displaced persons in Irpin near Kyiv.

Sustainability risks: Through a double-materiality analysis the Group identified climate-, social- and governance-related threats, split into physical and transition risks, alongside opportunities; ESG risks/opportunities inform strategy and financial planning and are entered in the risk register within the risk-management policy, with defined mitigation actions. Using national climate forecasts, the Group assessed location-specific physical and transition climate risks and their asset impacts over a horizon to 2050. Per scientific studies, Warsaw, Kraków and Wrocław will face rising numbers of extreme-heat days (Tmax ≥ 25°C), most acute in Wrocław (six more such days in 2050 than in the current decade), contributing to longer hot rainless periods and intensified urban heat-island effects. A further physical risk is rising mean annual precipitation (strongest in Kraków) and more days with rainfall >20 mm, increasing the probability of: river flooding in Warsaw, Kraków and Wrocław; sea flooding in Tri-City; and urban flash floods in Tri-City.

Dane dotyczące wypadków przy pracy, zdarzeń potencjalnie wypadkowych i sytuacji potencjalnie niebezpiecznych, złego stanu zdrowia oraz potwierdzonych chorób zawodowych pracowników są gromadzone za pomocą dedykowanej obszarowi BHP aplikacji eBHP oraz wewnętrznie prowadzonych rejestrów. Każdy pracownik lub współpracownik ma możliwość zgłoszenia zdarzenia za pośrednictwem aplikacji. Zgłoszenia trafiają bezpośrednio do Działu BHP, który podejmuje wymagane czynności związane z analizą i obsługą incydentu. Aplikacja umożliwia zgłaszanie wypadków oraz zdarzeń związanych ze stanem zdrowia pracowników, uzupełnianie zgromadzonych danych, generowanie oraz przechowywanie niezbędnych dokumentów, a także monitorowanie zgłoszonych przypadków oraz ich obsługę przez Dział BHP.  
Gromadzeniem i zarządzaniem danymi zajmują się osoby odpowiedzialne za obszar BHP, które na bieżąco analizują otrzymane zgłoszenia i podejmuje działania zgodne z obowiązującymi przepisami. Zgłoszenia dotyczące wypadków zarówno kadry własnej jak i kadry Podwykonawców są rejestrowane w dedykowanym module wypadkowym aplikacji, co umożliwia kompleksową ewidencję zdarzeń oraz efektywne zarządzanie danymi. Na budowach zgłoszenia wypadków podwykonawców dokonuje poprzez aplikację Kierownik Budowy, który następnie przekazuje je do systemu. W przypadku wypadków kadry własnej taką możliwość ma każdy pracownik i współpracownik lub kierownicy komórek organizacyjnych.  
Spółki z Grupy realizują działania wynikające z priorytetów Polityki Bezpieczeństwa i Higieny Pracy i Ochrony Środowiska (opisanej w S1-1). W zakresie BHP spółki Grupy pracują obecnie nad monitoringiem wdrażania Polityki i Standardu BHP. Są one stosowane w formie konkretnych klauzul w umowach, w szczególności w umowach ramowych, które wiążą Grupę z jej partnerami w perspektywie długoterminowej. Ponadto podejmowanie są działania, takie jak:  
- spotkania i szkolenia rozpoczynające pracę: kierownik budowy lub osoba przez niego wyznaczona omawia z pracownikami i pracownikami podwykonawców konkretne ryzyka związane z projektem przed  
rozpoczęciem prac, metody pracy, konkretne zagrożenia z zakresu BHP oraz środki ochrony indywidualnej, które mają być stosowane;  
- alerty i tzw. taski bezpieczeństwa: celem alertu bezpieczeństwa jest poinformowanie pracowników kadry, za pomocą krótkiego ogłoszenia/powiadomienia/ostrzeżenia/info rmacji, o konkretnych kwestiach związanych z bezpieczeństwem. Aby zapewnić, że alert bezpieczeństwa dotrze do każdego pracownika, jest on rozsyłany drogą mailową oraz jest dostępny na wewnętrznym intranecie;  
- alerty środowiskowe: celem alertu jest poinformowanie pracowników kadry oraz pracowników podwykonawców o konkretnych zagrożeniach związanych z prognozowanymi zdarzeniami ekstremalnymi (ulewne deszcze, intensywne opady śniegu, silne wiatry, upały), które mogą wpływać na pracę na placach budów;  
- − inspekcje/kontrole w miejscu pracy: co najmniej raz w tygodniu przeprowadzane są kontrole stanu BHP na budowach. Przeprowadzają je specjaliści BHP. Konkretne obszary robocze są sprawdzane pod kątem bezpieczeństwa, zdrowia i aspektów środowiskowych. Sprawdzane jest nie tylko bezpieczeństwo techniczne, ale także zachowania kadry własnej związane z bezpieczeństwem, takie jak zgodność z przepisami i stosowanie środków ochrony osobistej. Po kontroli sporządzane są raporty wraz ze sformułowanymi zaleceniami i wnioskami profilaktycznymi.  
- obserwacja (nie)bezpiecznych zachowań: obejmuje cotygodniowe obserwacje prowadzone przez Dział BHP mające na celu identyfikację nieprawidłowości w obszarze BHP. Obserwacje są następnie omawiane bezpośrednio z zainteresowanymi pracownikami. Wyniki są na bieżąco analizowane, czego skutkiem jest wdrożenie programu poprawy,  
- szkolenia z zakresu BHP oraz szkolenia z zakresu udzielania pierwszej pomocy dla wszystkich pracowników Spółki Dom Construction,  
- doposażenie wszystkich biur budowy Dom Construction w defibrylatory AED,  
- organizacja Dni Zdrowia obejmujących badania profilaktyczne na budowach Dom Construction.  
- W 2025 roku kontynuowano cykl komunikacji pt.  
- „Środa z dobrą praktyką”, mający na celu promowanie  
najlepszych praktyk bhp na budowach. Cyklicznie pracownicy budów otrzymują wiadomości wskazujące dobre przykłady działań, które mają inspirować innych oraz szerzyć wiedzę i pomysły na zwiększenie bezpieczeństwa na budowach.  
W roku 2025 przeprowadzono także zawody ratownicze, których celem było ćwiczenie i zarazem sprawdzenie wiedzy i umiejętności reagowania na sytuacje awaryjne mogące wystąpić na placu budowy podczas prac realizacyjnych. Pod koniec roku na budowach dodatkowo przeprowadzono dodatkowe szkolenie praktyczne z elementami technologii VR z zakresu gaszenia pożarów i ewakuacji.  
W ramach dobrej współpracy z organami państwowymi strażacy ze Specjalistycznej Grupy Poszukiwawczo-Ratowniczej w Warszawie, działającej w oparciu o Jednostkę Ratowniczo-Gaśniczą nr 15 Państwowej Straży Pożarnej, prowadzili na budowie Dom Construction ćwiczenia z zakresu zabezpieczenia osuwisk oraz wydobywania osób zasypanych w wykopach. Dom Construction udostępnił teren do ćwiczeń wraz ze specjalnie przygotowanymi w tym celu wykopami. Odbyło się także przeszkolenie dla pracowników Spółki z zasad postępowania i pierwszej pomocy w przypadku zasypania.  
We wszystkich lokalizacjach Dom Construction kolejny raz zostały zorganizowane Dni Zdrowia. Pracownicy podwykonawców mieli okazję porozmawiać ze specjalistami o zasadach dobrego żywienia, profilaktyce zdrowotnej, jak również zmierzyć sobie ciśnienie lub poziom cukru we krwi. Mieli również okazje wziąć udział w instruktażu z zasad udzielania pierwszej pomocy. W spółkach inwestorskich zorganizowano szkolenie z zasad udzielania pierwszej pomocy przedmedycznej.  
Wszyscy pracownicy Grupy mają obowiązek uczestnictwa w szkoleniach BHP (wstępnych, okresowych) organizowanych przez pracodawcę. Każda nowoprzyjęta osoba pierwszego dnia pracy uczestniczy w szkoleniu wstępnym, które przeprowadza pracownik Działu BHP lub osoba odpowiedzialna za ten obszar. Osoby, którym kończy się ważność szkolenia podstawowego uczestniczą w szkoleniach okresowych. Wtedy celem jest aktualizacja i uzupełnienie wiedzy i umiejętności, w szczególności z zakresu:  
- zagrożeń występujących w pracy oraz ryzyka związanego z nimi;  
- ochrony pracowników i tworzenia warunków pracy zgodnie z BHP;  
- metodyki prowadzenia instruktaży stanowiskowych i codziennych odpraw pracowników przed pracą (dla osób kierujących pracownikami);  
- postępowania w razie wypadków oraz w sytuacjach awaryjnych.  
W roku 2025 wdrożono przygotowane w Dziale BHP e-learningowe szkolenie okresowe BHP dla pracowników administracyjno-biurowych i kierujących pracownikami. Dzięki czemu obowiązkowe szkolenia okresowe BHP wymienionych grup stanowisk realizowane są wewnętrznie. Na potrzeby kadry budowy powstał autorski projekt „Budowa, bezpieczna przygoda” - projekt skierowany do kadry inżynieryjno-technicznej, mający na celu budowanie większej świadomości BHP u osób nadzorujących budowy.  
Wydatki Grupy Dom Development na działania z zakresu BHP w roku 2025 (prawie 4 mln zł)[26] wzrosły o 9% w porównaniu z rokiem 2024. W roku 2025 po raz drugi w historii działalności Dom Construction trzy budowy realizowane przez Spółkę wzięły udział w organizowanym przez Państwową Inspekcję Pracy  
konkursie „Buduj Bezpiecznie”. Celem konkursu jest promowanie wykonawców robót budowlanych, zapewniających wysokie standardy BHP w procesie realizacji obiektów budowlanych. Na poziomie etapu wojewódzkiego budowa Osiedle przy Forcie z Warszawy zajęła trzecie miejsce, budowa Osiedle Hubska z Wrocławia otrzymała drugie miejsce, a budowa Apartamenty Matecznego z Krakowa zajęła pierwsze miejsce w województwie małopolskim.  
W ciągu ostatniego roku poziom bezpieczeństwa w spółkach Grupy utrzymał się na takim samym, niskim poziomie. Różnica między ilością wypadków w miejscu pracy pracowników własnych i pracowników podwykonawców odzwierciedla różnice w wykonywanych zadaniach, świadomości bezpieczeństwa oraz wiedzy technicznej i doświadczeniu.

Dom Development Group sustainability report, Section 3 (S1-14 Occupational Health & Safety metrics). OHS KPIs presented as two-period comparison (current vs prior). Recordable work-related ill-health cases, own employees (employment contract/UoP): 2 vs 2 (flat). Lost days from work-related injuries, fatalities and ill-health among own employees (UoP): 57 vs 13 (sharp YoY increase). Value-chain fatalities (subcontractors) from work injuries/ill-health: 0 vs 2 (improvement). Recordable work-related ill-health cases among subcontractors: 9 vs no data. Recorded accidents among subcontractors: 12 vs no data. Fatalities among other on-site workers (collaborators, other employment forms): 0 vs no data. Recordable ill-health cases among other on-site workers (collaborators): 0 vs no data.

Accident, near-miss, hazardous-situation, ill-health and confirmed occupational-disease data collected via dedicated eBHP application plus internal registers; any employee/collaborator can report incidents, routed directly to OHS Department for analysis and handling. App supports reporting accidents and health-related events, data completion, document generation/storage, and case monitoring. OHS-responsible personnel manage and analyze submissions per regulations. Accidents of both own staff and subcontractor staff logged in dedicated accident module. On construction sites, subcontractor accidents reported via app by Site Manager, then forwarded to system; own-staff accidents reportable by any employee/collaborator or organizational-unit managers.

Group companies execute priorities of the OHS and Environmental Protection Policy (described in S1-1); currently developing monitoring of Policy and OHS Standard implementation, applied via contractual clauses, particularly framework agreements binding long-term partners. Measures include: pre-work meetings/trainings where Site Manager (or designee) reviews project-specific risks, work methods, OHS hazards and required PPE; safety alerts/tasks distributed by email and intranet; environmental alerts on forecast extreme events (heavy rain, snow, strong winds, heat) affecting site work; workplace inspections at least weekly by OHS specialists checking technical safety, worker behavior, regulatory compliance and PPE use, with post-inspection reports and preventive recommendations; weekly (un)safe-behavior observations by OHS Department feeding an improvement program; OHS and first-aid training for all Dom Construction employees; equipping all Dom Construction site offices with AED defibrillators; Health Days with preventive screenings on Dom Construction sites.

In 2025 continued "Wednesday with Good Practice" (Środa z dobrą praktyką) communication cycle promoting best OHS practices on sites. 2025 also held rescue competitions testing emergency-response skills; year-end additional practical training with VR technology elements covering firefighting and evacuation. In cooperation with state authorities, firefighters from the Specialist Search-and-Rescue Group in Warsaw (based on Rescue-Firefighting Unit No. 15 of the State Fire Service) conducted exercises on landslide securing and extraction of persons buried in excavations at a Dom Construction site; Dom Construction provided terrain with specially prepared excavations, plus employee training on conduct and first aid in burial cases. Health Days again organized at all Dom Construction locations; subcontractor workers consulted specialists on nutrition, health prophylaxis, blood-pressure/glucose measurement, and first-aid instruction; investor companies organized pre-medical first-aid training.

All Group employees must attend employer-organized OHS training (initial, periodic); new hires receive initial training day one from OHS Department; periodic training updates knowledge on workplace hazards/risks, worker protection and compliant conditions, methodology of workstation instruction and daily pre-work briefings (for supervisors), and conduct during accidents/emergencies. In 2025 implemented in-house OHS Department e-learning periodic OHS training for administrative-office staff and supervisors, enabling internal delivery of mandatory periodic training for these groups. Proprietary "Construction, a Safe Adventure" (Budowa, bezpieczna przygoda) project created for engineering-technical site staff to build OHS awareness among site supervisors.

Dom Development Group OHS expenditure in 2025 (nearly PLN 4M) rose 9% versus 2024. In 2025, for the second time in Dom Construction history, three Company-executed sites entered the State Labor Inspectorate "Build Safely" (Buduj Bezpiecznie) competition promoting high-OHS-standard contractors. At voivodeship stage: Osiedle przy Forcie (Warsaw) placed third; Osiedle Hubska (Wrocław) placed second; Apartamenty Matecznego (Kraków) placed first in Małopolskie voivodeship. Over the past year Group safety remained at the same low level; the difference between own-employee and subcontractor workplace-accident counts reflects differences in tasks performed, safety awareness, technical knowledge and experience.

Analiza istotnych ryzyk, wpływów i szans uwzględniła (oprócz podstawowych działalności Grupy dotyczących sektora budownictwa i nieruchomości) wpływy dla sektora pośrednictwa kredytowego i sektora apartamentów serwisowanych.

- sprawozdawczości finansowej (12 miesięcy),  
- Perspektywa średnioterminowa – perspektywa modelu biznesowego (odpowiada długości planowania, realizacji i sprzedaży inwestycji) = 2-3 lata  
- Perspektywa długoterminowa – perspektywa planowania = powyżej 3 lat  
Ze względu na specyfikę branży, dla Grupy perspektywa czasowa wynosząca powyżej trzech lat zawsze stanowi perspektywę długoterminową. Jest to okres wybiegający poza standardowe kroki realizowane przy danej inwestycji, tj.: jej planowanie, realizację oraz okres sprzedaży.  
Przyjęcie perspektywy 3-letniej nie zwalnia spółek Grupy z myślenia o takich zagadnieniach jak ryzyka klimatyczne, cykl życia budynków czy wdrażanie GOZ, których wystąpienie na przestrzeni dłuższej niż trzy lata jest dla Grupy oczywiste. Grupa podeszła do procesu według sposobu top-down. W pierwszej kolejności Grupa kolejno analizowała kwestie z listy ESRS1 AR16 (stanowiące punkt wyjścia do określenia istotnych zagadnień), następnie uzupełniła listę o charakterystyczne dla niej kwestie związane ze zrównoważonym rozwojem (na podstawie analiz wstępnych), po czym przypisała możliwe wpływy, ryzyka i szanse do tych zagadnień[4] . Ocena wpływów i ryzyk dotyczyła etapu przed podjęciem działań mitygujących (brutto).

Wykluczenie tematu zostało przeprowadzone w następstwie analizy modelu biznesowego, strategii biznesowej i łańcucha wartości na wstępnym etapie badania przez osoby odpowiedzialne za obszar ESG.

- a) dotychczasowe matryce istotności Grupy, publikowane w raportach niefinansowych i stworzone w oparciu o standard GRI[5] ,

Consolidated Sustainability Report, Section 3 (Phase 2: Identification of principal impacts) of GK Dom Development. The double-materiality analysis of material risks, impacts and opportunities covered, beyond the Group's core construction and real estate activities, the credit-brokerage sector and the serviced-apartments sector. Three business-driven time horizons were adopted: short-term = financial reporting period (12 months); medium-term = business-model horizon matching investment planning, execution and sale (2-3 years); long-term = planning horizon above 3 years. Given the industry, any horizon beyond three years is always long-term, extending past the standard investment cycle (planning, execution, sales). The 3-year framing does not exempt Group companies from addressing climate risks, building life-cycle and circular-economy (GOZ) implementation, all of which are implemented within a maximum medium-term (up to three years) window. These horizons informed risk study and financial-materiality assessment.

In 2025 the Group reviewed the double-materiality analysis results and partially revised the process; the next process revision is planned for 2026. A top-down approach was used: the Group first analyzed topics from the ESRS1 AR16 list (starting point for material topics), supplemented it with Group-specific sustainability issues based on preliminary analyses, then assigned potential impacts, risks and opportunities to these topics. Impact and risk assessment addressed the pre-mitigation (gross) stage. After analyzing the ESRS1 Appendix A material-topics table, topics not relevant to the Group's activities were excluded following analysis of the business model, business strategy and value chain by ESG-responsible personnel.

The working team conducting the materiality study included individuals with the best available knowledge of due-diligence processes (Director of Risk Management and Compliance), drawing on the firm's due-diligence procedures to assess ESG issues. Preliminary impact-identification analyses were based on: (a) the Group's prior materiality matrices published in non-financial reports built on the GRI (Global Reporting Initiative) standard; (b) sector materiality matrices under SIN (Non-Financial Information Standards); (c) issues established as material within existing due-diligence processes; (d) publicly available sector and industry materiality indices; and (e) analysis of scientific publications and literature on trends in the Group's sectors. Due-diligence assessment considered results of the Group's due-diligence process and procedures based on the ESG DOM 2030 Strategy, environmental decisions issued by administrative bodies, the Code of Conduct, GK Dom Development Policies, and Group actions to implement them. Materiality-assessment tools used included SASB Materiality Finder and MSCI ESG Industry Materiality Map.

A peer-group analysis of comparable companies was performed for both sectors; in 2025 the competitor analysis was conducted for the second time, based on material topics indicated in their ESRS-based non-financial reports. The study also used: (a) 2024 qualitative interviews (60 persons) with Group management; (b) 2024 external interviews (6 experts) covering architect education on sustainability and climate change, sustainable construction, building carbon-footprint calculation, market situation, circular economy and sustainable design; (c) 2024 external interviews (10 persons) with key Contractors; (d) 2025 analysis of 32 surveys completed by Group employees; (e) 2025 results of a meeting with 10 representatives of expert organizations, ESG bodies and NGOs, plus 3 surveys and a note completed after the meeting; (f) 2025 results of Group customer surveys (119 completed); (g) 2025 results of local-community surveys (16 completed).

The Group accounted for impacts in which companies are involved through their own activities or business relationships; some material impacts were incorporated into the ESG DOM 2030 Strategy and ongoing company operations. On climate-change topics, the Group reviewed its resources, operational processes and value chain to determine climate-related impacts, risks and opportunities. The analysis covered: own operations (review of construction and investment-design processes for climate adaptation, climate mitigation including greenhouse-gas emission reduction, and energy consumption); and the upstream value chain (analysis of suppliers and producers of building materials and equipment regarding their ability to deliver low-emission materials). For physical climate-risk assessment, the Group analyzed locations of its operations; location was the sole differentiating factor, so disaggregation applies only to climate-change adaptation impact, and no other factors affecting materiality assessment were identified.

XTB S.A. Capital Group Consolidated Annual Report 2025. Section covers management board composition, share ownership by managing/supervising persons, and remuneration policy.

Board member responsible for Risk Management ended term 1 July 2025; profile: graduated Wrocław University of Technology (M.Sc. Eng., 1994), doctoral studies in economics at Warsaw School of Economics (2011); held securities broker license since 1995; career across brokerage houses—DDM S.A. Wrocław (to 1997), CBM WBK S.A., Dom Maklerski BMT S.A. (to 1998), exchange broker/market-maker at CDM Pekao S.A. (from 1998, risk-management specialist from 2002), UniCredit CAIB Poland S.A. risk/compliance manager (2007–2010), ING TFI S.A. and ING Investment Management (Polska) S.A. senior risk/performance specialist (2010–2013), Director and risk expert for brokerage launch at PGE Dom Maklerski S.A. (2013–2014); appointed Director of Risk Management at XTB S.A. in 2014.

Direct shareholdings of managing/supervising persons as of 31 December 2025 and report date (shares; total nominal value PLN): Omar Arnaout, President of Board, 62,310 shares / PLN 3,116; Filip Kaczmarzyk, Board Member, 43,616 / PLN 2,181; Paweł Szejko, Board Member, 35,154 / PLN 1,758; Jakub Kubacki, Board Member, 25,632 / PLN 1,282; Bartosz Osiński, Board Member, 1,208 / PLN 60 (term commenced 1 December 2025).

Prior-period holdings as of 1 January 2025: Omar Arnaout 50,717 / PLN 2,536; Filip Kaczmarzyk 35,501 / PLN 1,775; Paweł Szejko 29,358 / PLN 1,468; Jakub Kubacki 20,995 / PLN 1,050; Andrzej Przybylski 5,829 / PLN 291 (term ended 1 July 2025). Year-over-year holdings increased for all continuing members.

Share-ownership changes during reporting period—incentive program acquisitions on 23 April 2025: Omar Arnaout subscribed 11,593 shares; Filip Kaczmarzyk 8,115; Paweł Szejko 5,796; Jakub Kubacki 4,637; Andrzej Przybylski 4,158.

Board members' functions in Group subsidiaries (as of 31 December 2025 / report date): Omar Arnaout—Board Member, XTB Mena Limited; Jakub Kubacki—Board Member, XTB Mena Limited and XTB Financial Services Ltd.; Filip Kaczmarzyk—Executive Director for Trading, XTB Limited (UK). Board members received no remuneration for subsidiary-governance roles in 2025 or 2024.

Remuneration policy: governed by the Fixed Remuneration Policy for Board and Supervisory Board members (31.07.2023), the Variable Remuneration Components Policy (12.04.2024), and the Incentive Program Regulations (12.04.2024); documents available on the Company's investor-relations corporate-governance page (https://ir.xtb.com/lad-korporacyjny/regulaminy-i-polityki/). Board remuneration model comprises fixed pay, variable pay, and non-monetary benefits; terms and amounts set by the Supervisory Board; members employed under indefinite-term employment contracts; remuneration set adequate to function and the Company's scale of operations.

Fixed remuneration reflects type of work, required qualifications, quantity/quality and assessment of work, and scope of organizational responsibility; Supervisory Board considers local labor-market conditions to ensure pay levels do not encourage excessive risk-taking to obtain the variable component.

Variable remuneration is an annual bonus contingent on management-objective achievement, dependent on balanced and risk-adjusted results of individual members, the Company, and Group; members are informed of objectives and assessment rules. The variable-to-fixed ratio may not exceed 200% per Board member, and not exceed 100% for the Board member responsible for Risk. Variable pay is disbursed in tranches reflecting the Company's long-term interests; the entire variable component is awarded in XTB own shares. At least 40% of variable components paid in financial instruments is deferred over three to five years (period set per business cycle, nature/risk of activity, and the individual's duties). Variable pay not exceeding the PLN equivalent of EUR 50,000 and ¼ of a Board member's total annual remuneration is not deferred. Where the individual's total prior-year remuneration exceeds the PLN equivalent of EUR 1,000,000, deferral applies to 60% of variable components. Free disposal of subsequent share tranches occurs after publication on the GPW of the consolidated annual report.
