Capital Group Consolidated Annual Report 2025 excerpt detailing General Meeting (Walne Zgromadzenie) procedures and shareholder rights under company Statut and Polish law (Public Offering Act, Reports Regulation). Voting rights: each share carries one vote; Statut grants no voting privileges; shareholder may vote differently with each held share. Proxy (pełnomocnik) may represent more than one shareholder and vote differently per shareholder's shares, must vote per shareholder instructions, and must disclose any actual or potential conflict of interest, in which case granting further proxy is impermissible. A shareholder may not vote, personally or by proxy, on resolutions concerning their own liability to the Company (including discharge/absolutorium, release from obligation, or disputes with the Company); this restriction does not bar voting as proxy for another shareholder on such matters. Participation rights: only persons who are shareholders sixteen days before the General Meeting date (record date) may participate. Holders of dematerialized bearer shares must request, from the entity maintaining their securities account, a personal certificate of participation rights, submitted no earlier than after announcement of the Meeting convocation and no later than the first business day after the record date. Holders of registered shares and temporary certificates, plus pledgees and usufructuaries with voting rights, may participate if entered in the share register on the record date. Right to propose draft resolutions: shareholder(s) representing at least one-twentieth (1/20) of share capital may, before the Meeting, submit draft resolutions in writing or electronically. Right to place matters on the agenda: shareholder(s) representing at least 1/20 of share capital may demand inclusion of specified matters in the next Meeting's agenda; the demand must reach the Management Board no later than twenty-one days before the Meeting and may be submitted electronically; the Board must announce agenda changes no later than eighteen days before the Meeting, in the manner proper for convening. Method of convening: the Meeting is convened by announcement on the Company website and in the manner specified for transmitting current information under the Public Offering Act, made at least twenty-six days before the Meeting date. The convocation announcement must contain in particular: date, time, place, and detailed agenda; precise description of participation and voting procedures; the record date; a statement that only persons who are shareholders on the record date may participate; and indication of where and how participants may obtain the full documentation/draft resolutions (or, where no resolutions are envisaged, comments of the Management Board or Supervisory Board on agenda matters), plus the website address where Meeting information will be available. Under the Reports Regulation, the Company must transmit via current report inter alia the date, time, place, and detailed agenda of the Meeting. For intended Statut amendments, current-report announcement covers existing provisions, proposed changes, and—where the scope is significant and the Company decides to prepare a new consolidated text—the new consolidated Statut text with enumeration of new provisions; draft resolutions and material annexes are likewise announced. Venue: General Meetings are held at the Company's registered seat. In 2025, Meeting proceedings were transmitted online via a dedicated website, whose address was indicated through the Company website no later than 7 days before the Meeting date. In 2025 no convocation announcement included information on the possibility of shareholders participating via electronic means of communication. Right to information / refusal: the Management Board refuses information if disclosure could harm the Company, an affiliated company, or a subsidiary company/cooperative, in particular by revealing technical, commercial, or organizational business secrets; a Board member may refuse where disclosure could ground criminal, civil, or administrative liability. Information provided to a shareholder must be made public via current report. A shareholder refused requested information during the Meeting who registered an objection to the minutes may apply to the registry court to compel the Board to provide it, within one week of the Meeting's conclusion; the shareholder may also apply to compel the Company to announce information provided to another shareholder outside the Meeting. Under the Reports Regulation, the Company must transmit via current report information provided to a shareholder pursuant to a registry court order in such cases. Right to demand copies of annual financial statements: every shareholder may demand copies of the Management Board's activity report and the financial statements, together with a copy of the Supervisory Board report and the statutory auditor's opinion, no later than fifteen days before the Meeting. Right to demand election of the Supervisory Board by separate-group voting: at the request of shareholders representing at least one-fifth (1/5) of share capital, the next General Meeting must elect the Supervisory Board by voting in separate groups.

Śródroczne skrócone skonsolidowane sprawozdanie finansowe zostało zatwierdzone przez Zarząd Jednostki dominującej w dniu 17 listopada 2025 roku.

W procesie stosowania zasad (polityki) rachunkowości Zarząd Jednostki dominującej dokonał następujących osądów, które mają istotny wpływ na przedstawiane wartości bilansowe aktywów i zobowiązań.

Na dzień bilansowy rocznego okresu sprawozdawczego przeprowadzany jest przegląd składników aktywów trwałych, w tym wartości niematerialnych w celu stwierdzenia, czy nie występują przesłanki wskazujące na możliwość utraty ich wartości. XTB S.A. Capital Group interim condensed consolidated financial statements, accounting-policy and judgment section of the Q3 2025 report. Statement of compliance: prepared under IAS 34 as endorsed by the EU, covering 1 January 2025 to 30 September 2025 with comparatives for 1 January to 30 September 2024 and the balance-sheet position as at 31 December 2024; consolidates the parent (XTB S.A.) and its subsidiaries. (in liquidation, described in note 1.2). Data comparable and prepared on consistent principles across all periods presented.

Group anticipates no material impact from any of the above.

Professional judgment: in applying accounting policies the parent's Management Board made judgments materially affecting carrying amounts of assets and liabilities. Significant estimates and valuations: IFRS preparation requires estimates and assumptions, continuously assessed by management, based on historical experience and other factors including reasonable expectations of future events; actual results may differ; estimate revisions recognized in the period of change (and future periods where applicable).

Expected credit losses and asset impairment: Group recognizes an ECL allowance under IFRS 9 for all assets measured at amortized cost, incorporating forecasts and expected future economic conditions in credit-risk assessment. Where objective evidence of impairment exists from events after initial recognition reducing expected future cash flows, write-downs are charged to current-period costs. Group assesses impairment of overdue receivables and provides for estimated impaired and uncollectible amounts. At the annual reporting date, non-current assets including intangibles are reviewed for impairment indicators (e.g., license expiry or withdrawal from use); where an indicator exists, a formal recoverable-amount estimate is performed, and where carrying amount exceeds recoverable amount, impairment is recognized and the asset written down to recoverable value.

XTB S.A. Capital Group 2025 Consolidated Annual Report excerpt covering the macroeconomic and capital-market environment. Eurozone: ECB ran accommodative policy amid easing inflation and moderate growth; H1 2025 continued the easing cycle, cutting key rates in March 2025—deposit rate to 2.50%, refinancing (main refi) rate to 2.65%, marginal lending rate to 2.90%—reacting to slower growth and disinflation. From September 2025 the Governing Council held rates steady: deposit rate 2.00%, refinancing rate 2.15%, reflecting inflation near the ~2% medium-term target. Eurozone real GDP growth projected ~0.9% (European Commission spring forecast), wider EU ~1.1%; eurozone headline inflation fell to ~2.1% in 2025, near the ECB ~2% target. European equity markets showed volatility mixed with solid rallies and moderate optimism; STOXX Europe 600 hit record highs in February 2026, exceeding 630 pts intraday (historic maximum), led by financials, commodities, banks and industrials. IPO activity rebounded: Q3 2025 saw over a dozen issues totaling >EUR 2.3bn, a clear YoY increase. Overall 2025 was a mixed year—optimism and index strength alongside episodes of elevated volatility.

Polish market: WIG broad index rose ~47% YoY, setting historic 2025 highs with broad sectoral gains across large, mid and small caps. Turnover grew alongside prices: full-year GPW main-market equity turnover ~PLN 470.3bn (+~42% YoY); average session equity trading value PLN 1.89bn (+~42% YoY). Record month December 2025: total equity turnover PLN 44.7bn (+76.2% YoY), of which order-book turnover PLN 38.2bn (+53.2% YoY). Liquidity growth driven by greater foreign and sustained domestic investor engagement; 2025 ranked among the strongest years for Polish equities in the decade.

Global environment (IMF/OECD): 2025 world growth moderate, readings mostly 3.1–3.4%; average global GDP ~3.2%, OECD real global growth ~3.1%, a slowdown vs pre-pandemic; 2026 growth expected to ease to ~3.0–3.1% amid trade restrictions, geopolitical tensions and weaker investment. Global CPI inflation stabilized ~3.6% in 2025 (down from prior highs), regionally varied—near central-bank targets in developed economies, slightly above in emerging markets. USA: GDP up ~2.2% (a slowdown); consumer CPI fell to ~2.7% late year, nearing the Fed 2% target; core inflation stabilizing, allowing neutral rates and cautious policy. China: GDP growth ~4.5%, among the highest of major economies despite real-estate and investment slowdown; CPI fell 0.1% YoY in May 2025 and 0.3% in September 2025, signaling near-zero/deflationary conditions, prompting the PBoC to prioritize growth support over inflation control.

Geopolitics: War in Ukraine—Russian forces crossed Ukraine's eastern, southern and northern borders on 24 February 2022; EU and other nations imposed severe sanctions targeting strategic Russian sectors by blocking access to technology and markets. No material direct impact on the Group, but it drove high volatility in financial and commodity markets, affecting XTB client transactional activity and Group results. Middle East conflict—early March 2026 escalation in which Iran attacked infrastructure in Dubai (UAE), causing major disruption to ~20% of global oil exports; oil prices rose 6–10% short-term, raising commodity/financial volatility and energy costs for firms and consumers. XTB holds two subsidiaries in Dubai; the company monitors the situation and sees no material negative impact to date. US trade policy—the Trump administration introduced significant tariffs in 2025, lifting the US average effective tariff rate from ~2.3% in early 2025 to ~9.8%–15% by year-end, influencing global trade and financial markets.

Consolidated Sustainability Reporting section E5-4 "Resources Used" (Inflows) for the Group, a multi-family residential developer. Consolidated Annual Report of XTB S.A. Capital Group 2025 (Management Board Report on activities of XTB Capital Group and XTB S.A. in 2025; Corporate Governance section, p.174). Excerpt covers risk-management framework and corporate-governance disclosures.

Risk management: Group sets early-warning limit thresholds for quantitative elements of the acceptable-risk-level declaration at levels stricter than the declaration itself. Breaching such limits triggers actions defined in contingency capital plans and contingency liquidity plans, aimed at reducing risk exposure and improving capital/liquidity position before risk exceeds risk appetite; on appetite breach, actions intensify and the Supervisory Board is informed immediately of every breach of the acceptable risk level.

Stress testing: key risk-management tool examining impact of low-probability, high-negative-effect scenarios on Company activity, covering internal threats and external factors (partner/counterparty problems and failures, possible penalties imposed by authorities supervising XTB across various areas). All stress tests run at least annually. Particular emphasis on tests measuring impact of unexpected, severe short-term market changes; given business specifics and maintenance of material open positions dependent on individual market-risk factors, XTB emphasizes such tests, performing single-factor stress tests assessing impact of a sharp material price change in one specific factor.

Liquidity management: Procedure permits exceptions to its application, requiring approval of at least two Management Board members of the Parent; exception information passed to Parent's Risk Control Department. Parent implemented contingency liquidity-maintenance plans, unused in the reporting and comparative periods because the most-liquid assets (own cash) significantly exceed liabilities. Heads of relevant Parent organizational units conduct ongoing supervision of cash deposited on account against planned operational liquidity needs; liquidity analysis considers current ability to obtain liquid funds, future needs, alternative scenarios and contingency plans. Risk Control Department also performs daily supervision/control over cash-account balances. Contractual payment terms of financial assets and liabilities presented in notes 36.3 (consolidated) and 37.3 (separate); partial and cumulative contractual liquidity gap (assets total minus liabilities total) given per maturity bracket.

Group manages financial resources via ongoing monitoring of ability to finance assets and meet obligations timely without loss. XTB liquidity-management objective: maintain on bank accounts sufficient cash to cover all necessary operations. For certain bank accounts tied to financial-instrument operations, Parent uses a liquidity model defining a safe free-cash zone requiring no corrective action; on reaching upper limit, Parent transfers surplus above optimal level to relevant current account; on reaching lower limit, transfers funds from current account to restore optimal cash level. Liquidity operations also executed by Trading Department and Finance & Accounting Department. Subsidiaries manage liquidity by analyzing expected cash flows and matching asset maturities to liability maturities; subsidiaries use no models; gap-analysis-based management deemed effective and sufficient; no liquidity incidents or inability to meet obligations occurred in subsidiaries.

Corporate governance: In 2025 XTB S.A. applied corporate-governance principles of "Best Practices of WSE Listed Companies 2021" ("DPSN 2021"), adopted by the Exchange Council via Resolution No. 13/1834/2021 of 29 March 2021. Current text available at WSE site (https://www.gpw.pl/dobre-praktyki2021); statement on compliance status published in Corporate Governance section of XTB investor-relations site (https://ir.xtb.com/). Report describes implementation of selected DPSN 2021 principles most significant to strategic goals, values, shareholders and clients.

Chapter 1 Information Policy and Investor Communication: Company applies principles of reliability and equal access to information for investors and shareholders; maintains and regularly updates websites: corporate (http://www.xtb.com/), investor relations (https://ir.xtb.com/), sustainability/ESG (https://esg.xtb.com/).

Legal basis for XTB S.A. corporate governance: applicable law (Minister of Finance Regulation of 6 June 2025 on current and periodic information disclosed by securities issuers and conditions for recognizing as equivalent information required by non-EU-member-state law; Journal of Laws 2025, item 755) plus DPSN 2021 and KNF Corporate Governance Principles for Supervised Institutions. Pursuant to §72(7)(5) of that Regulation (consolidated text, J.L. 2025, item 755), XTB S.A. Management Board presents its corporate-governance compliance statement for 2025.

# **2 OMÓWIENIE WYNIKÓW FINANSOWYCH DOM DEVELOPMENT S.A. I JEJ GRUPY**
## **AKTYWA**
W strukturze aktywów Grupy, podobnie jak w poprzednich latach, dominowały aktywa obrotowe, o wartości 5 729 mln zł według stanu na dzień 31 grudnia 2025 roku. Udział aktywów trwałych wyniósł zaledwie 4% sumy bilansowej. Stan gotówki rozumianej jako środki pieniężne i ich ekwiwalenty powiększone o środki na otwartych rachunkach powierniczych utrzymywał się na bardzo wysokim poziomie 522 mln zł, gwarantując Grupie elastyczność w reagowaniu na zmiany w otoczeniu rynkowym.  
Wartość środków na mieszkaniowych rachunkach powierniczych spółek z Grupy była relatywnie wysoka i na dzień 31 grudnia 2025 roku wyniosła 253 mln zł wobec 217 mln zł rok wcześniej. Wysoki poziom tych środków wynika z bardzo restrykcyjnych wymagań dotyczących momentu zwalniania tych środków z rachunków powierniczych na rachunek bieżący dewelopera, a wzrost odnotowany w 2025 roku jest w głównej mierze wynikiem zwiększonego wolumenu sprzedaży. Jednakże ciągle niewielki udział tych środków w relacji do wartości sprzedaży zafakturowanej ujętej w pozycji pasywów _„przychody przyszłych okresów”_ (ok. 12% na koniec 2025 i 2024 roku), świadczy zarówno o dużej sprawności operacyjnej spółek z Grupy jak i o terminowej realizacji budów, gdyż uwalnianie środków z otwartych deweloperskich rachunków powierniczych następuje proporcjonalnie do zaawansowania budowy, po osiągnięciu określonych etapów jej realizacji.  
Niezmiennie, kluczową pozycją w aktywach Grupy są zapasy, których udział w sumie bilansowej wynosił 85%, a ich wartość na przestrzeni 2025 roku wzrosła o 18% do poziomu 5 087 mln zł. Na tę pozycję bilansu składają się przede wszystkim projekty w budowie i grunty inwestycyjne zakupione pod przyszłe projekty o łącznej wartości 4 421 mln zł.

XTB S.A. Capital Group consolidated annual report 2025. Net interest result on client cash: 78.0M PLN in 2025, representing 3.6% of total Group revenue (2024: 3.1%), up 19.0M PLN YoY. Interest income on client cash rose 34.6M PLN (+32.7%) YoY, while interest expense paid to clients increased 15.5M PLN (+33.3%); the client free-cash remuneration product launched November 2023. Result on financial operations: (-)55.0M PLN in 2025, down 116.7M PLN versus prior year's positive 61.7M PLN, driven chiefly by negative FX differences of (-)93.1M PLN (mainly PLN appreciation against USD and EUR), plus interest income on own cash and held bonds totaling 39.3M PLN, down 13.1M PLN YoY due to lower deposit rates and lower bond yields.

Consolidated operating costs reached 1,313.7M PLN in 2025, up 427.0M PLN versus 886.7M PLN in 2024 (+48.2%). Marketing costs rose 240.1M PLN YoY (584.9M PLN vs 344.8M PLN, +69.6%) on higher online/offline campaign spend. Salaries and employee benefits up 101.4M PLN YoY (413.0M PLN vs 311.6M PLN, +32.5%) driven by headcount growth. Other external services up 53.6M PLN YoY (132.8M PLN vs 79.2M PLN, +67.7%), reflecting higher spend on (i) IT systems and licenses (+33.7M PLN), (ii) IT support services (+7.2M PLN), and (iii) market data delivery (+4.5M PLN). Commission costs up 10.1M PLN YoY (107.4M PLN vs 97.3M PLN, +10.4%) on larger amounts paid to payment service providers used for client deposits. Other cost lines: depreciation 25.4M PLN vs 19.9M PLN (+27.6%); other costs 23.6M PLN vs 12.8M PLN (+84.3%); taxes and fees 16.0M PLN vs 13.1M PLN (+21.7%); building maintenance and rental 10.6M PLN vs 8.0M PLN (+32.0%).

As of 31 December 2025, Group total assets stood at 9,086.7M PLN, up 2,441.0M PLN (+36.7%) versus end-2024 (6,645.6M PLN). Asset composition (31.12.2025 vs 31.12.2024): own cash 1,994.0M PLN vs 1,619.5M PLN (+374.5M PLN, +23.1%); client cash 5,864.4M PLN vs 3,751.3M PLN (+2,113.1M PLN, +56.3%); financial assets at fair value through profit or loss 1,007.0M PLN vs 1,123.9M PLN (-116.95M PLN, -10.4%); financial assets at amortized cost 107.8M PLN vs 55.0M PLN (+52.7M PLN, +95.8%); prepayments and accruals 29.0M PLN vs 19.7M PLN (+9.4M PLN, +47.5%); intangible assets 1.4M PLN vs 2.0M PLN (-0.6M PLN, -30.4%); property, plant and equipment 63.4M PLN vs 65.3M PLN (-1.9M PLN, -2.9%); income tax receivables 14.1M PLN vs 0.13M PLN (+14.0M PLN, +10,672.5%); deferred tax assets 5.6M PLN vs 8.7M PLN (-3.1M PLN, -36.2%); total assets 9,086.7M PLN vs 6,645.6M PLN (+2,441.0M PLN, +36.7%).

The most significant asset positions at both year-ends were Treasury-guaranteed cash and corporate bonds guaranteed by banks; cash plus bonds (presented within fair-value-through-profit-or-loss financial assets) comprised 86.5% of assets at end-2025 and 87.2% at end-2024. At 31 December 2025 the Group held no bonds (31 December 2024: 424.7M PLN). End-2025 own cash plus bonds fell 2.5% YoY, while client cash rose 56.3% YoY; the largest value increase in assets, 2,113.1M PLN, occurred in client cash. Cash comprises the Group's own cash and client cash; client cash is deposited in bank accounts separately from Group cash. XTB places part of its cash in bank deposits and financial instruments, i.e., government bonds and corporate bonds.

XTB S.A. Capital Group Consolidated Annual Report 2025 (ESG/social disclosures, ESRS S1). IBOR reform impact: the Group does not expect a material effect of IBOR reform on its financial liabilities but cannot conclusively determine the impact, as not all systemic and regulatory solutions have been developed. Management analyzed these amendments and concluded no material impact on the Group's financial position, results, or disclosure scope.

Published standards/interpretations not yet effective and not early-adopted by the Group: Amendments to IFRS 10 and IAS 28 on sale/contribution of assets between an investor and its associates or joint ventures, resolving inconsistency between IFRS 10 and IAS 28; accounting treatment depends on whether the assets/cash sold or contributed to the associate/joint venture constitute a "business" (full gain/loss recognized if a business; partial recognition limited to other investors' interests if not), EU endorsement of this amendment deferred as at the reporting date. Management is assessing the impact of the above standards on the Group's financial position, results, and disclosure scope and does not expect new/amended standards to have a material impact in the period of first application.

Consolidation Principles: Consolidated financial statements comprise the separate financial statements of Dom Development S.A. and those of its subsidiaries. Subsidiaries' statements, after adjustments to conform with IFRS, are prepared for the same reporting period as the parent using consistent accounting policies and uniform policies applied to like transactions and events; appropriate adjustments are made to eliminate any divergence in applied policies. All significant intra-group balances and transactions, including unrealized gains arising from intra-group transactions, are fully eliminated; unrealized losses are eliminated unless they evidence impairment.

Subsidiaries: Subsidiaries are consolidated from the date the Group obtains control until control ceases. Control by the parent exists where it holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiaries, more than half of voting power in the entity, unless it can be demonstrated that such ownership does not constitute control; control also exists where the Company can direct the entity's financial and operating policies. Changes in the parent's ownership interest that do not result in loss of control over a subsidiary are accounted for as equity transactions; in such cases the Group adjusts the carrying amounts of controlling and non-controlling interests to reflect changes in relative interests in the subsidiary. Consolidated Sustainability Reporting section of the Dom Development S.A. Capital Group Management Board report for fiscal year 2025 (Grupa Kapitałowa Dom Development S.A.), addressing climate risk analysis. The Group, drawing on available national climate-change projections, assessed which physical and transition climate risks could materialize at specific operating locations and how they could affect assets. The sole identified opportunity is an extended construction/investment window enabled by milder winters and higher temperatures. Climate risk analysis was conducted over a time horizon to 2050. Since 2021 the Group has measured its Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions and set a 2030 reduction target, forming the basis for transition-risk management.

Methodology comprised: (1) physical risk identification based on 21st-century climate-change scenarios for Poland prepared by IOS-PIB under the Klimada 2.0 project, scenario RCP 8.5 versus the 2011-2020 decade, plus Urban Adaptation Plans for Gdansk, Krakow, Warsaw and Wroclaw; (2) transition risk identification (regulatory, market, technological); (3) greenhouse-gas emissions assessment of Group Scope 1 and 2 emissions across prior years; (4) supplier-action assessment summarizing building-materials suppliers' emission-reduction and low-emission-materials efforts; (5) industry-regulatory benchmarking comparing Group practices against best practices in real estate and construction to identify mitigation and adaptation solutions. Identified threats, classified as physical and transition, plus identified opportunities, were entered into a risk register within the risk-management policy; ESG risks and opportunities are deemed critical to strategy and financial planning, with mitigation actions defined.

Transition risks - regulatory/legal. Threats include failure to respond to EU regulatory changes, specifically: amendments to the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD); CBAM (indirect upward pressure on prices of aluminium, steel, cement, ceramics, gypsum, lime); EU ETS extension to the heating sector from 2026 (indirect impact on heat-energy tariffs); EU Taxonomy (progressive building adaptation to technical screening criteria/TKK requirements); the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), requiring prevention of potential environmental and social impacts across the value chain; new rules restricting certain transport models with significant impact on company-operated infrastructure; and insurance-market changes stemming from legal shifts arising from the European Commission communication "Managing climate risks - protecting people and prosperity." Potential financial effects: increased operating costs (e.g., higher insurance premiums); revenue loss from stricter spatial-planning regulations and reduced demand for high-emission products; increased costs from tightened environmental regulations, potential litigation, fines and penalties, and rising non-financial reporting requirements - translating into higher land-acquisition costs or inability to purchase land, underestimation of execution costs at land-purchase date, higher investment-execution costs, valuation uncertainty, and greater cost pressure on subcontractors with possible need to expand headcount. Mitigation measures: continuous monitoring of environmental and non-financial reporting legal requirements; executing investments meeting all environmental/climate requirements; active participation in industry organizations and technical working groups and commenting on changing regulations; precise delegation of duties for identifying environmental regulatory aspects; oversight of validity and expiry of public-administration permits; defined procedures for updating or obtaining new permits; verification of environmental-report templates and submission deadlines; ongoing monitoring of regulatory and legislative processes; and monitoring of political developments to anticipate impacts.

Transition risks - market. Potential financial effects: increased CAPEX; reduced demand for high-emission products and services causing revenue loss; higher production costs from changing input prices (e.g., energy, water) and output costs (e.g., waste processing); increased costs from purchasing more advanced low-emission technology equipment and systems, business-process conversion and adaptation, and premature depreciation of high-emission equipment and materials; increased R&D investment and expenditure for new-technology implementation; and increased costs from climate-adaptation solutions and meeting changing customer preferences. Mitigation: strengthened cooperation and dialogue with value-chain participants; promotion and gradual deployment of low-emission solutions and materials; creation of industry/cross-industry partnerships promoting low-emission solutions; implementation of solutions reducing electricity, heat and water demand; and project-level materials-management plans to eliminate waste.

Transition risks - technological change. Threats: digitalization of operations and related risks (cybersecurity, business-continuity safeguards, unauthorized data access); failure to align IT systems with business and regulatory needs; requirement to incorporate changed heat-supply methods including renewable (OZE/RES) sources in investments; replacement of existing materials, equipment and fleet with lower-emission options; requirement to use lower-emission materials and other changes toward zero-emission building construction; engagement in innovations such as Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) for long-term renewable energy use; potential shortening of owned-asset life cycles - earlier impairment and withdrawal or write-off of high-emission machinery, equipment and fleet; and rising costs from potential full fleet electrification.

XTB S.A. Capital Group Consolidated Annual Report 2025, corporate governance section detailing Supervisory Board committees and Management Board composition. The entire Supervisory Board serves as both the Risk Management Committee and the Remuneration Committee. In 2025 the Risk Management Committee held five meetings and adopted 4 resolutions; average member attendance was 100%. Individual attendance: Jan Byrski N/A (no meetings during his term), Aleksander Chłopecki 100%, Bartosz Zabłocki 100%, Grzegorz Grabowicz 100%, Katarzyna Dąbrowska 100%, Ewa Stefaniak 100%, Jakub Zabłocki 100%. Risk Management Committee duties: drafting the brokerage house's risk-appetite document; opining on the Management Board's risk-management strategy; supporting the Supervisory Board in overseeing the Board's execution of that strategy; reviewing the remuneration policy and its implementation for alignment of the pay system with the firm's risk exposure, capital, liquidity, and the probability/timing of income; discussing and approving the Acceptable Risk Level Declaration; and discussing and approving the ICAAP report. Remuneration Committee duties: supporting the Management Board in preparing remuneration solutions consistent with the Variable Remuneration Components Policy; opining on and reviewing the remuneration policy including amounts and components; supervising payouts of variable remuneration to staff materially affecting the firm's risk profile; and setting variable remuneration components of Management Board members per that policy. The Supervisory Board may by resolution appoint additional committees and set their composition.

Risk Management Committee composition at 1 January 2025: Jan Byrski (Chairman), Grzegorz Grabowicz, Katarzyna Dąbrowska, Ewa Stefaniak, Bartosz Zabłocki (all members). Composition at 31 December 2025: Aleksander Chłopecki (Chairman), Grzegorz Grabowicz, Katarzyna Dąbrowska, Ewa Stefaniak, Bartosz Zabłocki, Jakub Zabłocki (members), indicating the chairmanship transferred from Byrski to Chłopecki and Jakub Zabłocki joined during the year.

Management Board changes in 2025: On 31 March 2025 the Company received a declaration from Andrzej Przybylski that he would not seek appointment for another Board term; consequently his term as Management Board Member for Risk Management expired 1 July 2025 (current report no. 5/2025 of 31.03.2025). On 25 June 2025 the Supervisory Board resolved to appoint a new-term Management Board of four members for a joint three-year term running 2 July 2025 to 2 July 2028, comprising: Omar Arnaout (President/CEO), Paweł Szejko (Member), Filip Kaczmarzyk (Member), Jakub Kubacki (Member). On 26 August 2025 the Supervisory Board resolved to appoint Bartosz Osiński as Management Board Member for Risk, conditional on Polish Financial Supervision Authority (KNF) approval; KNF approval was received 1 December 2025.

Management Board with first-appointment and current-term-expiry dates: Omar Arnaout (President), first appointed 10.01.2017, term expires 02.07.2028; Filip Kaczmarzyk (Member), 10.01.2017, 02.07.2028; Paweł Szejko (Member), 28.01.2015, 02.07.2028; Jakub Kubacki (Member), 10.07.2018, 02.07.2028; Bartosz Osiński (Member), Supervisory Board appointment date 26.08.2025 with KNF approval received 1 December 2025, term expires 02.07.2028. Post-balance-sheet event: on 3 March 2026 the Company received Jakub Kubacki's resignation from his Management Board Member position, effective end of 30 June 2026.

Governance framework: The Management Board is the managing body, operating under the Board Bylaws, meeting at least monthly at the Company's registered office (or elsewhere in Poland with all members' consent). Appointment/removal rules and powers are set by the Company's Articles of Association (published at https://ir.xtb.com). The Board comprises three to six members, including the President and two Vice-Presidents; at least two members must hold higher education, at least three years' work experience in financial-market institutions, and a good reputation regarding their functions. Members are appointed and removed by the Supervisory Board, which sets the number of members in its appointment resolution; a member may also be removed or suspended by General Meeting resolution. Members serve a joint three-year term; mandates expire at the General Meeting approving financial statements for the last full financial year of their function and in other cases under the Commercial Companies Code. Management Board competences cover conducting the Company's affairs and representation, and all matters not reserved by law or the Articles to the General Meeting or Supervisory Board; the Board makes decisions in the Company's interest, drafts development-strategy proposals, and defines the Company's main objectives. The President convenes and chairs Board meetings (and may authorize other members to do so); in the President's absence the oldest member convenes meetings.

XTB S.A. Capital Group Consolidated Annual Report 2025, sustainability statement section. Foreword signed by Paweł Szejko, Member of the Management Board for Finance, citing market recognition: four XTB good practices featured in the latest Forum Odpowiedzialnego Biznesu (Responsible Business Forum) publication, and the "ESG Company of 2024" title awarded at the Invest Cuffs conference, affirming consistency, engagement and transparency build stakeholder credibility.

Reporting comparability (BP-2): no change in 2025 versus 2024 base year in data collection, aggregation or presentation methods, except recalculation of 2024 greenhouse gas emissions (Chapter 2.1.3). Where GHG emission data unobtainable, estimation method applied; value-chain metrics also estimated via indirect sources. Group did not depart from ESRS 1 section 6.4 medium- and long-term time horizons; despite carbon-footprint estimates, no metrics or monetary amounts identified as high-uncertainty.

Sustainability reporting governance (GOV-5): annual sustainability statement prepared by the Sustainability Team, a unit within XTB S.A.'s Finance, Accounting and Administration Department—placement intended to ensure consistency and integrity with financial reporting. Non-financial reporting project managed by the Sustainability Manager, who mobilizes organizational resources, collects and analyzes data across all Group units, and works closely with advisor and auditor. Highest decision-making link is the Member of the Management Board for Finance, the Board's representative in the process. Double materiality assessment in 2024 identified an opportunity (improved reporting quality strengthening stakeholder relations) and a legal/reporting risk (failure to adapt to highly volatile legislative environment or improper fulfillment of reporting obligations), mitigated via early/full preparation, legislative monitoring, qualified staff and external advisors, and training. First data-verification link: named employees of subsidiaries, branches and XTB S.A. departments supplying timely quality data and audit evidence; second link: the Sustainability Team, which consolidates and verifies unit data; followed by sustainability assurance. Carbon-footprint calculation reliability additionally assured by external advisor Fundacja Climate&Strategy.

Competence development of corporate bodies in 2025: the Member of the Management Board for Finance completed two courses on sustainability reporting standards, requirements/application examples, and reporting analysis, run by the Education Center of the Polish Chamber of Statutory Auditors (Polska Izba Biegłych Rewidentów). One member of the XTB S.A. Supervisory Board completed ACCA training "ESG in Finance. Due diligence in reporting environmental topics in ESRS."

Governance and supervision (GOV-1, section 1.2): describes composition of XTB S.A. bodies, the parent entity for branches and subsidiaries influencing their strategy and operations. The Management Board performs the executive function—representing and conducting XTB S.A.'s affairs, drafting development strategies and defining main business objectives. Management Board change in 2025: Mr. Andrzej Przybylski resigned from his Management Board position (previously responsible for risk at XTB); effective 01.12.2025, with Polish Financial Supervision Authority (KNF) consent, Mr. Bartosz Osiński assumed the position of Member of the Management Board for Risk (further details in Chapter 4.2.1). The Management Board is the highest sustainability-management instance; Paweł Szejko, Member of the Management Board for Finance, delegated for direct sustainability management and supervision per the Internal Regulations of the Finance, Accounting and Administration Department, ensuring consistency between non-financial and financial reporting via single-person oversight.

In 2025 two teams were established within the division: the Sustainability Team (ESG development, ESG reporting, ESG Strategy execution) and the Social Projects Team (pro-employee, pro-environmental actions and financial education aligned with XTB's business model and the XTB Foundation). Environmental, governance and social criteria are considered in ongoing Board management; sustainability topics addressed at Board meetings as needed. # **3 SKONSOLIDOWANA SPRAWOZDAWCZOŚĆ ZRÓWNOWAŻONEGO ROZWOJU**
## _Zatrudnienie i relacje z pracownikami_
Grupa Dom Development dokłada należytej staranności w zakresie utrzymywania dobrych relacji z pracownikami, prowadząc działalność w zgodzie z obowiązującymi przepisami prawa pracy oraz standardami praw człowieka. Grupa traktuje wszystkich pracowników na równi, szanując i doceniając ich różnorodność.  
Podstawowym dokumentem regulującym kwestie pracownicze jest Strategia Zarządzania Kapitałem Ludzkim. Ten wewnętrzny system regulacji określa priorytety i cele dotyczące zarządzania zasobami ludzkimi, stanowiąc integralną część ogólnej strategii biznesowej. Dokument opisuje misję i priorytety HR, koncentrując się na byciu pracodawcą pierwszego wyboru, budowaniu długoterminowych relacji opartych na zaufaniu oraz tworzeniu zaangażowanego środowiska pracy. Kluczowe obszary strategiczne obejmują zarządzanie kompetencjami, oferowanie atrakcyjnych warunków zatrudnienia, pozyskiwanie najlepszych kandydatów oraz model HR wspierający operacje i komunikację wewnętrzną. Strategia ta jest zgodna z międzynarodowymi wytycznymi dotyczącymi praw człowieka i zasad pracy, w tym Deklaracją MOP oraz wytycznymi OECD.  
Polityka Zatrudnienia dopełnia i uszczegóławia kwestie ujęte w Strategii. Głównym celem Polityki jest określenie ram, zasad i celów zatrudnienia, rozwoju zawodowego, utrzymania równowagi między życiem zawodowym a prywatnym (work-life balance), a także wspieranie reintegracji zawodowej i społecznej. Polityka dąży do stworzenia przejrzystego i sprzyjającego rozwojowi środowiska pracy, w którym członkowie Personelu (osoby zatrudnione na podstawie umów o pracę i umów cywilnoprawnych) są doceniani i zaangażowani. Ma ona również na celu zapewnienie zgodności z obowiązującymi przepisami prawa oraz promowanie zdrowej równowagi między życiem zawodowym a prywatnym, równości, elastyczności i dialogu.  
Kwestie bezpieczeństwa i higieny pracy reguluje przyjęta w Grupie Polityka Bezpieczeństwa i Higieny Pracy i Ochrony Środowiska. Dokument ma na celu stałe podnoszenie standardów w zakresie ochrony środowiska, zdrowia, bezpieczeństwa i higieny w całej Grupie oraz wspiera identyfikację i minimalizację ryzyk obrażeń ciała i zdrowia wszystkich osób, na które wpływ ma Grupa – pracowników, klientów, członków społeczeństwa. W ramach dopełnienia należytej  
staranności na placach budów regularnie (co najmniej raz na tydzień) odbywają się przeglądy BHP. Pracownicy biorą także udział w szkoleniach z zakresu bezpieczeństwa oraz udzielania pierwszej pomocy. W 2025 roku opracowane zostały alerty klimatyczne, które mają zapewnić ochronę zdrowia i bezpieczeństwa pracowników oraz minimalizować ryzyka wynikające z ekstremalnych zjawisk pogodowych. Alerty rozsyłane są do pracowników przez Zespół Raportowania Niefinansowego w sytuacji ogłaszania alertów przez IMGW bądź RCB dla danego regionu.

# **3 SKONSOLIDOWANA SPRAWOZDAWCZOŚĆ ZRÓWNOWAŻONEGO ROZWOJU**
## _Środowisko_
Grupa prowadzi swoją działalność w zgodzie z obowiązującymi regulacjami w zakresie ochrony środowiska i klimatu. Nadrzędnym wewnętrznym dokumentem regulującym kwestie środowiskowe jest Strategia ESG DOM2030, która określa cele Grupy do roku 2030.  
Przyjęta Polityka Bezpieczeństwa i Higieny Pracy i Ochrony Środowiska ma na celu identyfikację i minimalizację zagrożeń dla środowiska naturalnego, wynikających z prowadzonej działalności biznesowej. Polityka odnosi się m.in. do takich kwestii jak: zapobieganie zanieczyszczeniom, redukcja ilości odpadów oraz zapewnienie efektywnego wykorzystania materiałów, energii i wody oraz stosowanie materiałów lokalnych i naturalnych o niższym śladzie węglowym. Należyta staranność w zakresie realizacji postanowień polityki obejmuje:  
- dokonywanie przeglądów działalności w celu identyfikacji problemów, które mogą mieć znaczący wpływ na środowisko,  
- minimalizowanie ryzyka wystąpienia zdarzeń środowiskowych poprzez procedury zarządzania ryzykiem,  
- utrzymywanie zdolności do reagowania w sytuacjach kryzysowych,  
- angażowanie łańcucha dostaw  
- zapewnienie niezbędnej świadomości i szkoleń pracownikom na wszystkich szczeblach,  
- zapewnienie, że każdy projekt będzie posiadał plan gospodarowania odpadami. Polityka podlega regularnemu przeglądowi.  
Polityka Zrównoważonych Zamówień Grupy ma na celu zarządzanie łańcuchem dostaw w sposób odpowiedzialny, wspierając tym samym zobowiązanie Grupy do zrównoważonego rozwoju i realizację założeń strategii ESG DOM 2030. Polityka ma na celu m.in. komunikowanie dostawcom oczekiwań wynikających ze strategii ESG DOM 2030 oraz prowadzenie efektywnej i partnerskiej  
współpracy, uwzględnianie w decyzjach zakupowych kryteriów środowiskowych, społecznych oraz dotyczących ładu korporacyjnego (ESG) oraz dążenie do równowagi pomiędzy opłacalnością biznesu a szeroko pojętym interesem społecznym i odpowiedzialnym w zarządzaniu procesami zakupowymi.  
W ramach realizacji Strategii ESG DOM 2030, w 2025 roku Grupa wdrożyła Standard Zrównoważonych Zamówień. Głównym celem tego dokumentu jest określenie zasad realizacji polityki zakupowej Grupy. Kluczowe cele Standardu obejmują:  
- zmniejszenie negatywnego wpływu działalności Spółki na środowisko naturalne poprzez promowanie produktów i usług o niższym wpływie na środowisko,  
- zwiększenie efektywności kosztowej zakupu materiałów i usług, obniżenie kosztów operacyjnych, a także wdrażanie zasad projektowania pod kątem obiegu zamkniętego w celu zwiększenia trwałości inwestycji,  
- wspieranie Kontrahentów we wdrażaniu zasad ESG.  
Dopełnienie należytej staranności w zakresie kwestii środowiskowych jest możliwe dzięki realizacji działań określonych w Środowiskowym Planie Awaryjnym. Dokument jest standardem Grupy i stanowi dokument wdrożeniowy. Określa on sytuacje stanowiące potencjalne zagrożenie. Plan dotyczy terenów wszystkich budów oraz działań wykonywanych przez Grupę oraz jej Podwykonawców. Za wdrożenie dokumentu odpowiada Koordynator ds. ESG. Plan podlega także corocznej weryfikacji przez Dyrektora ds. BHP i Koordynatora ds. ESG.

# **3 SKONSOLIDOWANA SPRAWOZDAWCZOŚĆ ZRÓWNOWAŻONEGO ROZWOJU**
## _Zwalczanie przekupstwa i innych form korupcji_
Polityka Antykorupcyjna, Prezentowa i Konfliktu Interesów jest rozwinięciem ogólnej zasady całkowitego odrzucenia i potępienia wszelkich działań przejawiających objawy korupcji w bieżącej działalności biznesowej spółek z Grupy. Główne założenia i cele Polityki to:  
− minimalizacja ryzyka korupcyjnego Celem wdrożenia jest jak najdalej idąca minimalizacja prawdopodobieństwa uczestnictwa osób zaangażowanych we współpracę biznesową ze Spółką w procederach o charakterze korupcyjnym.  
− zarządzanie ryzykiem braku zgodności Polityka stanowi jeden z instrumentów służących dochowaniu należytej staranności w zarządzaniu ryzykiem braku zgodności.  
− wymóg uczciwości  
Spółka wymaga od wszystkich osób zaangażowanych we współpracę biznesową bezwzględnie uczciwego i w granicach prawa sposobu postępowania.  
− zapobieganie konfliktom interesów Wprowadzane są rozwiązania mające na celu zapobieganie Konfliktowi interesów.  
Polityka szczegółowo reguluje zasady antykorupcyjne dotyczące zarówno członków Personelu, jak i Partnerów biznesowych, zasady przyjmowania  
i wręczania prezentów mające minimalizować ryzyko korupcji, a także kwestie związane z identyfikowaniem zagrożeń korupcyjnych, ochroną konkurencji oraz zarządzaniem konfliktem interesów.

# **3 SKONSOLIDOWANA SPRAWOZDAWCZOŚĆ ZRÓWNOWAŻONEGO ROZWOJU**

W Polityce Grupa zobowiązuje się m.in. do wykorzystywania różnych kanałów komunikacji w celu kontaktu z interesariuszami, regularnego zbierania informacji zwrotnych i terminowego odpowiadania na nie terminowo, rzetelnie i przejrzyście. Section 3 Consolidated Sustainability Reporting of Grupa Dom Development, covering employment/labor relations, environment, anti-corruption, competition, and consumer interests.

Employment and labor relations: Group maintains labor relations per applicable labor law and human rights standards, treating all employees equally and valuing diversity. Primary governing document is the Human Capital Management Strategy, an internal regulatory system defining HR priorities/objectives as integral to overall business strategy; mission centers on being employer of first choice, building long-term trust-based relationships, and creating an engaged work environment. Key strategic areas: competency management, attractive employment terms, acquiring top candidates, and an HR model supporting operations and internal communication. Strategy aligns with international human rights/labor guidelines including the ILO Declaration and OECD Guidelines. Employment Policy complements the Strategy, framing rules/objectives for employment, professional development, work-life balance, and vocational/social reintegration; covers Personnel on employment and civil-law contracts, promoting transparency, equality, flexibility, and dialogue. Occupational Health, Safety and Environmental Protection Policy aims at continuous improvement of environmental, health and safety standards and minimization of injury/health risks to employees, clients, and the public. OHS reviews conducted on construction sites at least weekly; employees participate in safety and first-aid training. In 2025 the Group developed climate alerts to protect employee health/safety and minimize extreme-weather risks, distributed by the Non-Financial Reporting Team upon IMGW or RCB regional alerts.

Environment: Group operates per environmental/climate regulations. Overarching internal document is the ESG DOM2030 Strategy, setting Group goals through 2030. The OHS and Environmental Protection Policy targets identification/minimization of environmental threats, addressing pollution prevention, waste reduction, efficient use of materials/energy/water, and use of local/natural lower-carbon-footprint materials. Due diligence includes activity reviews to identify significant environmental impacts, risk-management procedures, crisis-response capability, supply-chain engagement, employee awareness/training at all levels, and a waste-management plan for every project; policy reviewed regularly. Sustainable Procurement Policy manages the supply chain responsibly, supporting ESG DOM 2030, communicating supplier expectations, incorporating ESG criteria in purchasing decisions, and balancing profitability with social interest. In 2025, under ESG DOM 2030, the Group implemented a Sustainable Procurement Standard defining procurement-policy execution, with goals: reducing negative environmental impact via lower-impact products/services; increasing cost-efficiency of material/service purchases, lowering operating costs, and applying closed-loop (circular) design principles to extend investment durability; and supporting contractors in ESG implementation. Environmental due diligence is enabled through the Environmental Emergency Plan, a Group standard/implementation document defining potential threat situations, applicable to all construction sites and activities of the Group and its subcontractors. Implementation is the responsibility of the ESG Coordinator; the plan undergoes annual verification by the OHS Director and ESG Coordinator.

Anti-corruption: The Anti-Corruption, Gifts and Conflict of Interest Policy extends the principle of total rejection/condemnation of corruption in Group business. Main objectives: minimization of corruption risk (reducing likelihood of involvement by business partners in corrupt practices), management of non-compliance risk, requirement of integrity from all parties in business cooperation (lawful, honest conduct), and prevention of conflicts of interest. Policy regulates anti-corruption rules for Personnel and business Partners, gift acceptance/giving rules to minimize corruption risk, identification of corruption threats, protection of competition, and conflict-of-interest management.

Competition: The Good Practices Policy for stakeholder relations defines rules for open, transparent dialogue with contractors/business partners, shareholders, local communities, clients, and other stakeholders. The Group commits to using various communication channels, regularly collecting feedback and responding timely, reliably, and transparently, and providing only true and complete information about its operations. The document is integral to organizational culture and serves as a non-compliance risk-management instrument; implementation/updating is the responsibility of the Risk Management and Compliance Director, with oversight of application across companies by the company Management Board.

Consumer interests: The Good Practices Policy for Stakeholder Services contains detailed client-service commitments protecting consumers, particularly residential-unit buyers. Key aspects: 1. legal compliance and financial protection of buyers; 2. transparency and reliability of offer and communication; 3. service process and risk management; 4. handover and after-sales service; 5. complaints and dispute resolution. The Group commits to measuring/monitoring client satisfaction and ensuring convenient service conditions, including individual solutions for clients in difficult life situations.

The Management Board of XTB S.A. is the highest decision-making body on ESG risks; ESG risks identified under double materiality, consistent with the 2024-2027 strategy, were incorporated into the internal risk management system. Responsibility for completeness, reliability and correctness of reporting data rests with experts across Group business areas; the Sustainability Team coordinates the ESG reporting process, collecting, consolidating and analyzing information using common company-wide tools. XTB S.A. Capital Group Consolidated Annual Report 2025. Product portfolio detail for tax-advantaged retirement and savings accounts and a multicurrency eWallet.

IKE account: opened/funded exclusively in PLN; purchases of non-PLN instruments incur currency conversion fee per current tariff; offers investment in 7,200+ equities and a dozen-plus ETFs; idle funds bear interest at prevailing rates. IKZE account: individual (non-shared), available to persons 18+, including sole proprietors, with Polish tax residency; key benefit is deductibility of contributions from PIT taxable base, granting current-year tax relief; statutory annual contribution cap tied to average wage; withdrawal after retirement age (and minimum contribution period) subject to 10% flat-rate tax; opened/funded only in PLN; offers 9,100+ equities and ETFs; idle funds interest-bearing.

UK ISA: targeted at persons aged 18-39 holding a National Insurance number and tax-resident status; XTB offers UK clients a Flexible Cash and Stocks & Shares ISA variant permitting withdrawal and re-deposit within one tax year without affecting the annual contribution limit. Cash ISA: UK tax-free savings account on which interest is exempt from tax; openable by persons 18+ resident in the UK for tax purposes; current aggregate cap of GBP 20,000 per tax year across all ISA accounts; balances may be interest-bearing; depending on Cash ISA type, withdrawable anytime or only after a fixed term; principal advantage is exemption of interest income from tax.

PEA: French long-term tax-preferential investment account; available to adults tax-resident in France; standard deposit limit EUR 150,000; funds investable in European company shares and selected qualifying funds and ETFs.

eWallet: multicurrency-card wallet supporting cashless in-store payments, mobile and contactless transactions, and worldwide ATM cash withdrawals; supports accounts in 25 currencies (EUR, USD, PLN, GBP, CZK, RON, HUF, CAD, YUAN, AUD, DKK, SGD, TRY, SEK, CHF, YEN, THB, NOK, MXN, BRL, MYR, MVR, LKR, TZS, INR) plus fast free inter-account transfers; instant access to funds; card issued under Mastercard license by DiPocket UAB, an Electronic Money Institution registered by the Bank of Lithuania; available to individuals holding an XTB investment account; currently offered to clients in Poland, Czech Republic, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Germany, France, Spain and Italy.

Macroeconomic environment. XTB Group performance is driven by macro conditions and global market volatility; inflation, interest rates, FX rates and international events shape client behavior, investment appetite, and product preferences. High inflation erodes real purchasing power, steering investors toward capital-protecting instruments across asset classes (exchange-listed equities, ETFs, CFDs, corporate and government bonds, structured products, real-estate and commodity funds). Interest-rate changes affect financing cost, deposit/bond attractiveness, and expected returns, directly shaping capital allocation and medium-/long-term savings strategies. Global political/economic events (US trade-policy shifts, armed conflicts, geopolitical tensions) generate market volatility, move FX and asset prices, and determine client activity and XTB financial results.

Poland macro. In 2025 the Polish economy operated amid stabilizing macro conditions and gradual easing of inflationary pressure. Per preliminary GUS data, real GDP growth for full-year 2025 reached 3.6% y/y, a clear acceleration from 3.0% in 2024, confirming stronger economic activity dynamics across the year; growth supported chiefly by private consumption and recovering investment activity. Inflation declined steadily month-over-month through 2025; GUS preliminary CPI reading was 2.4% y/y in November 2025, a material slowdown versus earlier months. Monetary policy was cautious: in H1 the NBP reference rate held at 5.75%, reflecting prior monetary tightening; as inflation outlook improved, the Monetary Policy Council (RPP) began easing, cutting rates in H2 to approximately 4.25%. Per European Commission forecasts, Poland's 2026 real GDP growth is projected at approximately 3.5% amid stable private consumption and increased EU-fund-related investment; CPI inflation seen further fading to an annual average of approximately 2.9%, near the NBP target.

_Wpływ czynników makroekonomicznych na oszacowania oczekiwanych strat kredytowych dla portfela pożyczek Wonga_  
Oczekiwane straty kredytowe w odniesieniu do udzielonych pożyczek wycenianych według zamortyzowanego kosztu - wyznaczane są przy wykorzystaniu parametrów: PD (prawdopodobieństwa zdarzenia default (ang. default), rozumianego jako stan niewykonania zobowiązania), PPS (prawdopodobieństwa przedpłaty), LGD (straty pod warunkiem default) oraz EAD (ekspozycji na moment default).  
Parametr LGD uzależniony jest od odzysków realizowanych po wystąpieniu zdarzenia default. Odzyski na portfelu z utratą wartości realizowane są poprzez sprzedaż wierzytelności lub prowadzenie procesu windykacji polubownej, a następnie sądowej. W przypadku procesu windykacji prognozowane odzyski na potrzeby ustalenia parametru LGD bazują na historycznej krzywej wpłat dla podobnych wierzytelności i są okresowo weryfikowane oraz aktualizowane w razie istotnych zmian. Spółka Wonga w I połowie 2025 r. zaktualizowała wykorzystywaną krzywą wpłat, z uwagi na obserwowane w dłuższym horyzoncie czasu wyższe odzyski.  
Spółka dokonuje analizy wpływu czynników makroekonomicznych na planowane odzyski oraz oczekiwane straty kredytowe dla udzielonych pożyczek wycenianych według zamortyzowanego kosztu. Analizowane zmienne makroekonomiczne to:  
- bankructwo konsumenckie,  
- poziom bezrobotnych (zarejestrowanych ogółem, nowo zarejestrowanych, zarejestrowanych po raz kolejny),  
- stopa bezrobocia rejestrowanego,  
- nowe oferty pracy w okresie.  
W przypadku stwierdzenia poprawy dokładności prognozy z wykorzystaniem powyższych zmiennych makroekonomicznych (oprócz stosowanego skoringu behawioralnego) - są one dodawane do modelu szacowania strat kredytowych.  
_Wpływ czynników makroekonomicznych na oszacowania oczekiwanych strat kredytowych dla portfela pożyczek Novum_  
W obliczeniach oczekiwanych strat kredytowych uwzględnia się szacunki dotyczące oczekiwanego otoczenia makroekonomicznego. Wpływ czynników makroekonomicznych jest uwzględniany poprzez ujęcie wpływu prognozowanych zmiennych makroekonomicznych na wartości poszczególnych parametrów ryzyka (PD, LGD). Na podstawie danych historycznych weryfikowana jest zależność zmiany wartości tych parametrów lub ich składowych od zmiennych makroekonomicznych.  
Zakres analizowanych zmiennych makroekonomicznych uwzględnia następujące pozycje:  
- dynamika indeksu PKB,  
- zmiana wskaźnika cen (CPI),  
- zmiana indeksu sprzedaży detalicznej,  
- dynamika przeciętnych wynagrodzeń w gospodarce narodowej,  
- stopa bezrobocia.  
_Raport półroczny – Skrócone śródroczne skonsolidowane sprawozdanie finansowe_  
Na koniec 2024 r. istotnymi statystycznie zmiennymi makroekonomicznymi była dynamika wskaźnika cen CPI oraz zmiana stopy bezrobocia, które skorelowane były z historycznymi wpłatami, będącymi składowymi w szacunkach parametru LGD. Bazowy scenariusz prognozy makroekonomicznej, który został ujęty w szacunkach parametrów LGD opiera się na dostępnych prognozach makroekonomicznych, w szczególności na publikowanych przez Narodowy Bank Polski projekcjach inflacji i PKB.

Supervising persons held no shares or rights thereto (unchanged from prior report).

Material proceedings: Group companies Alupol Packaging S.A. and Alupol Packaging KĘTY Sp. z o.o. (Flexible Packaging Segment) imported aluminium foil for packaging from Thailand in 2021-2022, treated as Thai-origin goods supported by certificates of origin from Thai state authorities. In 2023 these transactions were subjected to customs-fiscal audits by the Silesian Customs-Fiscal Office in Katowice and the Pomeranian Customs-Fiscal Office in Gdynia, which—contrary to the companies' position and evidence—found the EU export resulted from the foil producer relocating activity from China to Thailand solely to evade anti-dumping and countervailing measures on Chinese aluminium foil. Based on issued decisions, customs liabilities of PLN 37.2M plus interest of PLN 11.5M were imposed; these were settled within the statutory deadline in 2024. The companies disagree, citing selective/arbitrary evidence assessment, and filed appeals to second-instance bodies; during 2025 second-instance decisions upheld the first-instance rulings. The companies then challenged the decisions in full before the Provincial Administrative Courts in Gdańsk and Gliwice, alleging baseless questioning of goods' origin and lack of evidentiary proceedings; appeals concern over a dozen customs decisions. The Provincial Administrative Court in Gliwice set 28 October 2025 as the hearing date for the first of the Group's appeals.

XTB S.A. Capital Group Consolidated Annual Report 2025, strategic outlook section addressing megatrends, regulatory environment, organizational structure, and sustainability across short- (1-2 yr), medium- (3-5 yr), and long-term (5+ yr) horizons. Digitalization: Company identifies long-term focus on mobile applications and digital platforms enabling fast, intuitive personal finance management, investing, and portfolio analysis, anticipating new business models and innovative investment products; notes generational shift as younger investors increasingly adopt digital tools demanding simplicity, transparency, and rapid information access. Cites Fintech Market Statistics and Forecast 2026-2034: global fintech market valued at USD 253.4bn in 2025, projected to reach USD 938.7bn by 2034 at ~15% CAGR.

Cybersecurity (short-term): References KPMG finding that 83% of firms in Poland experienced at least one cyberattack attempt in 2024; CrowdStrike European Threat Landscape Report 2025 indicating European firms were targets of nearly 22% of all ransomware attacks.

Legal/regulatory environment: Short-term factor is evolving national and European regulation requiring rapid compliance, corporate governance, and data security implementation. Highlights EU Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), adopted to harmonize crypto-asset market rules across member states, introducing new licensing requirements, increased market transparency, and stronger investor protection. Polish law remains unadapted to MiCA, preventing introduction of crypto-assets to the domestic-market offering, which generates over 50% of Group revenues. Additional short-term factor: binding recommendations from national financial supervisors (e.g., Spain restricting permissible financial-product advertising). Medium-term (3-5 yr): legal-environment changes at national/EU level may significantly determine pace and manner of new-technology deployment and scope of digital solutions, especially in fintech, AI, and investment platforms; growing importance of AI-use regulations governing decision algorithms, automated data analysis, and investment-support tools, plus increased consumer/investor protection (heightened disclosure requirements, product transparency, data security). Long-term (5+ yr): rising importance of regulations on reporting, transparency, and compliance standards, requiring continued development of internal processes, control systems, and cooperation with supervisory bodies.

Organizational structure (short-term): Group XTB employs and collaborates with 1,516 people worldwide under employment contracts, B2B contracts, and other agreements; decided to reorganize a business area at this development stage. Medium-term: focus on organizational culture built on efficiency and employee competencies, particularly IT, data analysis, cybersecurity, and modern investment tools; strengthening cross-team (business/operational/technological) collaboration and training/knowledge-management programs. Long-term: cyclical review of workforce/collaborator management, adaptation of organizational structure and work models to market/technological changes, competency monitoring, and building an attractive, stable employer brand.

Sustainability (short-term): Core development element; reporting aligned with EU ESRS standards, to which XTB has adapted and will continue adapting after final standard changes are implemented into Polish law. Encompasses Environmental (E), Social (S), and Governance (G) actions. Group executes its ESG Strategy targets over the 2024-2027 horizon, builds employee awareness via internal communication, and strengthens stakeholder dialogue including via ESG website https://esg.xtb.com/. Over the coming two years the Group will summarize Strategy execution, plans to set further milestones and goals, and will verify progress.

XTB S.A. Capital Group 2025 Consolidated Annual Report, Section 3 "Society," subsection 3.1 "Our Employees" (ESG/ESRS S1 disclosure). Workforce defined as Group XTB staff on employment contracts (direct employer influence) plus non-employees forming own workforce resources engaged via B2B contracts and civil-law agreements. Group employs and cooperates with over 1,500 people worldwide, reflecting >20 years of organizational culture development. Employee satisfaction high: 84.6% would recommend XTB as a good workplace (survey end-2024). XTB emphasizes work-life balance via flexible, competitive employment terms and a needs-adjusted benefits package; provides OHS (BHP) training and regular first-aid courses. Double-materiality analysis showed no significant human-rights impacts; commitments detailed in Chapter 2.2.3 Minimum Safeguards and in the Diversity Management, Equal Treatment and Inclusion Culture Policy (DEI). Promotion/employment decided on competencies.

Structural changes in the Talent (HR) area improved data quality for pay-gap indicator calculation. Identified material impacts, risks, opportunities (IRO) in tables in Chapter 1.6; key risks/opportunities/strategy linkages disclosed there. In 2025 material workforce impacts/risks/opportunities were reviewed but not substantially changed (minor editorial edits only); survey results consulted with all employee representatives to confirm ESRS topics cover all material workforce matters - no objections raised. 2025 employee initiatives (partly with XTB Foundation): "Inner Power" passion-sharing workshops; sports (WizzAir Prague Night Half-Marathon, Prague Five run, chess, badminton, office yoga, football, basketball); XTB picnic, Children's Day at HQ, Christmas gathering; cancer-prevention screenings ("Pink October," "Movember"); whole-Group participation in "Two Hours for Family" (XTB became international ambassador of this work-life-balance campaign); annual first-aid training; flu vaccination at HQ; employee volunteering ("Clean River," Cyprus beach cleanup and tree planting, Szlachetna Paczka/Noble Gift Pack).

Communication improvements: bilingual communications, intranet, xPress employee newsletter, "Town Hall" meetings, internal mailing; direct access to supervisors and Management Board members; cyclical online meetings where the CEO communicates financial results and strategic plans. Disclosures SBM-3 / S1-1: in 2025 XTB executed its 2024-2027 ESG Strategy, updated in 2024 based on stakeholder opinion survey within double-materiality assessment. Workforce representatives participated in workshops and in-depth interviews, identifying material impacts, risks and opportunities (described in ESRS 2 SBM-3, Chapter 1.6). Strategic targets set jointly with staff responsible for the workforce area, who drive operational delivery and report progress to the Sustainable Development Team. Double-materiality identified positive impacts (employment flexibility, cooperation with employee representatives, implemented policies/regulations ordering the workforce area) and negative actual/potential impacts (wage differences/pay gap; insufficiently developed internal communication lagging behind the Group's dynamic growth). The pay gap, first calculated for Group XTB in 2024, drove strengthened internal communication (xPress newsletter, regular Town Halls) and reinforcement of the remuneration area, including establishment of a dedicated remuneration organizational unit.

Headcount metrics (Total employees): 31.12.2024 = 1,015; 31.12.2025 = 1,315; growth +30% YoY. By gender at 31.12.2025: 791 men, 385 women, and 1 person not identifying as woman or man (vs 31.12.2024: men 0->1 line reflects "other" category +100%/+1; women 347->437, +26%; men 668->877, +31%). Group workforce at 31.12.2025 male-dominated. By contract type: permanent (indefinite) contracts 913 (2024) -> 1,177 (2025), +29% YoY, representing 90% of Group employment, growth dynamic close to total headcount growth; fixed-term contracts 102 (2024) -> 138 (2025), +35% YoY, growth dynamic 5 percentage points above total employment growth; employees not guaranteed working hours = 0 in both periods. Comparative gender sub-breakdowns show women +23%/+49% and men +32%/+28% across categories. "Other"/not-disclosed gender categories largely unchanged (bz.) except the single non-binary employee added in 2025.

_Raport kwartalny – Skrócone śródroczne skonsolidowane sprawozdanie finansowe_  
_Wpływ czynników makroekonomicznych na oszacowania oczekiwanych strat kredytowych dla portfela pożyczek Wonga_  
Oczekiwane straty kredytowe w odniesieniu do udzielonych pożyczek wycenianych według zamortyzowanego kosztu - wyznaczane są przy wykorzystaniu parametrów: PD (prawdopodobieństwo niewykonania zobowiązania), PPS (prawdopodobieństwo przedpłaty), LGD (strata z niewykonania zobowiązania) oraz EAD (ekspozycja na moment niewykonania zobowiązania).  
Parametr LGD uzależniony jest od odzysków realizowanych po wystąpieniu niewykonania zobowiązania. Odzyski na portfelu z utratą wartości realizowane są poprzez sprzedaż wierzytelności lub prowadzenie procesu windykacji polubownej, a następnie sądowej. W przypadku procesu windykacji prognozowane odzyski na potrzeby ustalenia parametru LGD bazują na historycznej krzywej wpłat dla podobnych wierzytelności i są okresowo weryfikowane oraz aktualizowane w razie istotnych zmian. Spółka Wonga w okresie 2025 r. zaktualizowała wykorzystywaną krzywą wpłat, z uwagi na obserwowane w dłuższym horyzoncie czasu wyższe odzyski.  
Spółka dokonuje analizy wpływu czynników makroekonomicznych na planowane odzyski oraz oczekiwane straty kredytowe dla udzielonych pożyczek wycenianych według zamortyzowanego kosztu. Analizowane zmienne makroekonomiczne to:  
- bankructwo konsumenckie,  
- poziom bezrobotnych (zarejestrowanych ogółem, nowo zarejestrowanych, zarejestrowanych po raz kolejny),  
- stopa bezrobocia rejestrowanego,  
- nowe oferty pracy w okresie.  
W przypadku stwierdzenia poprawy dokładności prognozy z wykorzystaniem powyższych zmiennych makroekonomicznych (oprócz stosowanego skoringu behawioralnego) - są one dodawane do modelu szacowania strat kredytowych.  
_Wpływ czynników makroekonomicznych na oszacowania oczekiwanych strat kredytowych dla portfela pożyczek Novum_  
W obliczeniach oczekiwanych strat kredytowych uwzględnia się szacunki dotyczące oczekiwanego otoczenia makroekonomicznego. Wpływ czynników makroekonomicznych jest uwzględniany poprzez ujęcie wpływu prognozowanych zmiennych makroekonomicznych na wartości poszczególnych parametrów ryzyka (PD, LGD). Na podstawie danych historycznych weryfikowana jest zależność zmiany wartości tych parametrów lub ich składowych od zmiennych makroekonomicznych.  
Zakres analizowanych zmiennych makroekonomicznych uwzględnia następujące pozycje:  
- dynamika indeksu PKB,  
- zmiana wskaźnika cen (CPI),  
- zmiana indeksu sprzedaży detalicznej,  
- dynamika przeciętnych wynagrodzeń w gospodarce narodowej,  
- stopa bezrobocia.  
Na koniec 2025 r. istotnymi statystycznie zmiennymi makroekonomicznymi była dynamika wynagrodzeń, która skorelowana była z historycznymi wpłatami, będącymi składowymi w szacunkach parametru LGD.  
_Raport kwartalny – Skrócone śródroczne skonsolidowane sprawozdanie finansowe_  
Bazowy scenariusz prognozy makroekonomicznej, który został ujęty w szacunkach parametrów LGD opiera się na dostępnych prognozach makroekonomicznych, w szczególności na publikowanych przez Narodowy Bank Polski projekcjach inflacji i PKB.

Macroeconomic impact — Novum loan portfolio: ECL incorporate expected macroeconomic environment via projected variables affecting risk parameters (PD, LGD), with historical-data validation of dependencies. Analyzed variables: GDP index dynamics, CPI change, retail sales index change, average national wage dynamics, unemployment rate. At end-2025 the statistically significant variable was wage dynamics, correlated with historical payments feeding LGD estimates. Baseline macro forecast scenario for LGD parameters relies on available projections, notably National Bank of Poland (NBP) inflation and GDP projections.

Loans granted measured at fair value — book value movement FY2025 vs FY2024: opening balance 3.3M PLN (prior 5.6M); repayments (2.9M) (prior (3.9M)); interest income 1.1M (prior 2.0M); revaluation 0.8M (prior (0.5M)); closing balance 2.3M PLN (prior 3.3M).

Interest-rate risk: profit/(loss) before tax sensitivity to a +/-50 basis-point shift in interest rates over the 12-month period ended 31.12.2025 is +/-PLN 12.879M (a 50bp decrease impacts -PLN 12.879M / shown as (12,879); a 50bp increase +PLN 12.879M), versus a corresponding (33) figure for the comparative 31.12.2024 period; figures in PLN thousands. Credit risk defined as unexpected default or deterioration of creditworthiness threatening obligation performance. Identified credit-risk scenarios: (1) Failure/insolvency of the bank holding the firm's or clients' cash — loss of access to deposited funds would weaken liquidity, force recovery from the bank's bankruptcy estate (lengthy, possibly incomplete), trigger client claims for amounts exceeding deposit-guarantee scheme coverage, and in extreme cases force XTB's own insolvency; mitigants include qualitative pre-onboarding bank vetting (market position, capital, reputation, repayment capacity, e-banking reliability/liquidity/security/functionality, banking diversification requirement, credit quality, legal/market practices on client-cash custody), ongoing credit-quality monitoring of open accounts, minimum required external agency credit ratings plus an insolvency-probability warning threshold, and limits curbing excessive cash concentration (including client funds) within one capital group. (2) Loss of securities held in XTB accounts — depositary malfunction revealing that client-held financial instruments do not exist; XTB pursues recovery from the depositary (time-consuming, possibly incomplete), faces client claims, risking liquidity/capital deterioration and inability to meet obligations; mitigants restrict depositaries to high-reputation, established entities operating under jurisdictions regulating third-party custody and supervised by competent authorities, with annual assessment of the depositary and its named sub-depositaries (credit quality, internal/external custody regulations). (3) Dependence/lack of diversification or excessive exposure to a single entity or related entities — technical problems at a credit institution could block access to funds for hours/days; prolonged financial distress or insolvency of an entity/capital group holding material own or client cash could cause liquidity and capital disruptions, in extreme cases inability to meet obligations; mitigants set a concentration limit on own funds within one capital group and monitor exposure and credit quality per entity. Market risk under market-maker model: XTB acts as counterparty to client-opened transactions, so financial results depend on open positions in individual instruments and market parameters. Sudden price movements and price gaps in underlying instruments can abruptly reprice XTB's open positions, generating material losses, increasing liabilities to clients (risking liquidity pressure from mass withdrawals), and sharply raising capital requirements necessitating position hedging; disruptions to hedging capacity become more likely; clients face heightened risk of rapid loss of funds (especially under high leverage) as position valuations fall and positions are closed for insufficient margin (stop out); mitigants include client/instrument/order limits, automated exposure monitoring, and triggering hedging transactions once limits are breached. Volatility and volatility-regime-change risk: volatility underpins the economic rationale for CFD trading and XTB's business model, but can increase potential market-risk loss, raise internal-capital requirements based on VaR methods, necessitate hedging of exposed positions, amplify period-to-period earnings swings, and increase hedging costs from maintaining higher margin deposits with liquidity providers; mitigants comprise VaR methodology, sensitivity analyses, stress tests, and dynamic adjustment of risk parameters (limits, exposure, hedging rules). Basis/imperfect-hedge risk: hedging a market-risk-exposed position via transactions based on a similar but non-identical underlying can generate losses from valuation divergence between the client-originated instrument and the hedging instrument; mitigants include hedging-instrument selection rules, limits on instruments and asset classes, and correlation and sensitivity analysis under extreme scenarios.
